speechtext: House again in Committee on Bill (No. 85) respecting forest reserves and parks.- Mr. Oliver.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This Bill was before the committee on a previous occasion, when somewhat full explanations were made in regard to it, and a map was laid upon the table which would give, perhaps, a clearer explanation than anything I could say. That map will be laid on the table again in a few minutes. Unless another resume of the purposes of the Bill is required, I would suggest that it be taken up clause by clause.
The minister might explain the general purposes of this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have just stated that I explained the Bill at some length on a previous occasion, but if another explanation is required, of course, I can repeat. The Bill is practically a revision of the present Forest Reserves Act. Perhaps the most important feature of it is that which sets apart by statute the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains as a forest reserve. Certain parts of that area are now under reservation. The Rocky Mountains Park, of which Banff is the capital, is a reservation by Act of Parliament-a park reservation, not a forest reserve. The Waterton Lakes reserve is a reserve by Act of parliament. The large area of which Jasper House might be called the capital is under reservation by order in council as a forest park. It is proposed to place the whole of the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains, including these reservations, in the position of a forest reserve, under restrictions as to surface occupation and regulations as to the protection of timber which prevail in regard to all other forest reserves under the present Forest Reserves Act. But this Bill contains a provision which differs from the existing Forest Reserves Act in this-that any portion of the area included in a forest reserve may be placed under the additional

restrictions or provisions which would enable that particular area to be used as a park or pleasure resort. These are the two distinctive features of the Bill.
Does the government own all the timber that is going to be protected?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There may be some small isolated areas taken up by settlers. There are certain small areas which we propose to take out of reservation. On examination it has been found that they do not meet the conditions considered desirable in a forest reserve, and we think the public interest is best served by withdrawing them. Besides the reserves shown on the main map, there are reserves in the railway belt of British Columbia which are shown on another sheet.
Is there not a reserve on the American boundary of Alberta? And has not some effort been made to have some other regulations on both sides of the line?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
None that have come to my attention. Any representations that have been made have looked to securing the setting apart of the reservation on our side. With that done, perhaps some question of uniform regulations might come up.
On section 2,-lands in schedule withdrawn from sale and occupancy,
What area is included in these reserves, and of the total what portion is on the Rocky mountains' slope?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under this Bill there are twenty-four reserves, with an aggregate area of 16,760,640 acres, as compared with twenty-one reserves, with an area of 3,379,200 acres under the present Act.
Within those sections that are set apart and are within these boundaries, are there any private ownerships, leases or anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are some mineral claims in this proposed Rocky Mountain reservation, and there may be an occasional settler. But the number of settlers is very limited, and of course their right would have to be dealt with; and there are some timber limits.

As the minister is aware, there are a number of settlers in some of these reserves, and is it the intention of the government to let them remain in peaceful possession where they are now, or to remove them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It depends on circumstances. If the settlers have gone upon the reservation after it was declared a reservation, then they are not recognized as having any right, and are subject to summary Mr. OLIVER.
removal. But if there are settlers now in legitimate occupation of land covered by a reservation at the time the reservation is declared, then of course they are dealt with on the basis of that right, whatever it may be. There is no intention or desire on the part of the government to interfere unduly with any man's right. But if parliament, in its wisdom, sanctions the action of the government in setting apart a certain reservation, and if, in pursuance of the purpose of parliament, it becomes necessary to clear that area of settlers, then of course that clearance must be effected, always having due regard to the value of the rights of the settlers. If a man has a right, and it is the will of parliament that he shall not retain that right, then he must be compensated.
I understand these reserves will only be declared as such when this Bill becomes law. There is no declaration of reservation yet, is there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These lands will only become a reservation when this Bill becomes law. But there are now a number of reservations under the existing Act which will be included under the terms of this Act when it becomes law. In the territory that is put under this Act, rights existent at the time of the passing of the Act of course must be recognized.
Are there any timber limits held under license and abutting on these reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there are timber licenses both abutting on the reserve and included in the reserve. The owner of a timber license would be in just the same position as the owner of a mineral right or a surface right. Whatever rights he had he would retain, or else be compensated for them.
Do I understand the minister to say that the holder of a timber license may still retain his right in that reservation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
These timber licenses will not be expropriated by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It has not been the policy to expropriate them. Of course we propose to handle the timber question in these reservations when we get to it, and have the means, and we propose to handle the timber question in a more detailed manner than we have yet been able to do. But up to the present time, we have not interfered with the right of limit holders whose limits happen to be included in the various reserves. Of course they aie subject to more

stringent regulations in regard to preservation from fire than the general regulations governing reserves. So far as they have a proprietary right, we have not interfered and do not propose to interfere with that right.
Will the minister tell the House how many acres of timber reserves there are in this portion now set off?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I would be safe in saying that the area is the difference between the area of the existing reserve, and the total area of the proposed reserve; that is to say, roughly speaking, the area of the Rocky Mountain forest reserve, if my information is correct, will be about 13,000,000 acres.
Does the minister mean to say that of this whole reserve of 16,000,000 acres odd, some 13,000,000 acres are already held by timber licensees?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no.
That is the question I asked.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not answer that question offhand. But I would say that the land held by licensees at the present time is not all in proportion the proposed total area.
Approximately.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think I could give that just now. The area of this reservation is very large, it includes the whole of the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains. Therefore, the area that could possibly be timbered under conditions suitable for commercial operations is very small as compared with the total area.
Has the minister any information which he could give to [the House as to the proportion of that which is timbered?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not now, but I could get it. We have gone into the matter fully, we have very detailed information, and any question in regard to the area or quantities I can give at a later date.

What the House ought to have, and what would be useful, is, in the first place, the area which is fairly well timbered, and the area which is not timbered but which is suitable for planting or forestation. These two figures put together would give us the area suitable for forest land. We might have 16,000,000 acres and a very small proportion, or a comparatively large proportion of it, might be land which might be useful for the purpose for which a forest reserve was set apart, namely, that timber may toe grown on it, and that all the atmospheric and climatic effects may be gained from it.
I suppose that these timber licenses were granted before these reserves were set apart?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. SCHAFFNER, Have any been granted since?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
And will not be?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And will not be. We do not propose to hold the timber which is in these forest reserves from use, but we propose to inaugurate a policy which will look to the utilization of the timber and to the reforestation or continued forestation of the land. We have not arrived at that point yet but we hope to do so. In a great measure the public requirements are met by the holders of timber licenses inside and outside the forest reserves, but our purpose, in dealing with the timber in the reserves is, first, the economic utilization of the timber which is useful for commercial purposes and, next, the reproduction of timber so that there shall be a continuous supply.

That puts a little different face upon the question of these timber reserves and rather changes our ideas. What is the primary object that the minister has in mind in setting apart these timber reserves?
Mr. OLIVER, The primary object is to conserve the sources of water supply by the protection and production, or reproduction, of timber or wood around the sources of the water supply. It is to be supposed that the sources are elevated areas, otherwise hills, and, they being elevated areas, are not the most desirable areas for agricultural purposes. We propose to utilize that land which is, under ordinary conditions, either waste or of much lesser value in this work of conserving the water supply, and at the same time to reproduce the timber growth for the benefit of the dwellers on the prairies surrounding these areas.

I understand that the primary object in setting apart these reserves is to conserve moisture and rainfall. What idea can the minister have in his mind when he wants to utilize the tintber that is at present growing on these reserves? The minister must not lose sight of the fact that if this timber is once utilized it will toe very difficult if not impossible to reproduce it. I think that the minister will agree with me that that will be the result in the case of most of these reserves. If what the minister has stated is the primary object, it seems to me that it is not good policy that this timber should be utilized, and that he should depend upon



tlie reproduction of tlie timber for the purpose of conserving moisture. I cannot see what good object the minister has in his mind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, we are quite aware that we cannot eat our cake and have it too, that we cannot take coal out of a coal mine and still have the coal mine; but we do know that we can grow wheat on a certain area one year, harvest the crop, grow wheat again on that same area next year and continue the process indefinitely. So, by the present existence of forest growth and the proved adaptability of the area to the growth of forest trees, we have hoped and we believe, judging from the experience of other countries, that we will be in a position to harvest our crop of timber and reproduce that crop.

How long does it take to reproduce average kinds of timber?
I assume that it takes some years anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It depends upon the kind of timber. Poplar will reproduce in fifteen or twenty years, spruce takes much longer and other kinds of timber will take a still longer time. I am not ^ suggesting that we can harvest our crop this year and again harvest another crop next year. We have to take it according to the term of years that intervenes before the next crop will be matured, but still I believe it is possible to harvest those trees in the forest which have attained their maturity, or their reasonable maturity, leaving the trees which have not yet attained that maturity to be harvested within a few years after that when they shall have attained their maturity. With a tree, as with an animal, or with any crop, up to a certain period of its life, its growth will be faster than at any other period, so that, after having arrived at a certain period in life, whether it be an animal or a tree, the growth will be very slight. We believe that when a tree has arrived at the period when its growth has done its quickest work in the production of timber, that is the time to harvest the crop and leave room for the neighbouring tree also to come up to that standard of growth. That is the theory of forestry as I understand it.

The minister has undertaken quite an important work, and he will require to use a very great deal of judgment as to which of the reserves he shall utilize in the manner he has stated. Certainly none of the reserves on the prairie can be utilized in that way. I have brought the question of our own Turtle Mountain reserve before the House on several occasions, but I shall not say anything particularly with regard to it to-day. I may say that the policy of the minister in retaining these timber

areas for the purpose of conserving moisture is a very laudable one, indeed, and one to which governments might long ago have given their attention with beneficial results, but I am not much in favour of a policy of destroying the timber on these reserves, and depending upon the reDroduction of the forest growth. I think the minister will have to use a great deal of judgment in deciding as to what timber he shall destroy. What he says about the life of a tree, and the life of a man is all very well, but the comparison does not extend any great distance. I repeat, that it will require a great deal of judgment as to what timber shall be destroyed in the expectation that it will reproduce itself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite appreciate everything that my hon. friend has said, and I may say that we are hastening slowly in this matter. We are studying the conditions as they exist in our own country. We have a vast mass of information with regard to forestry, and forest reproduction in other countries. What applies in other countries may not apply in our own, and for that reason we are studying the question very carefully to see what the possibilities are. We hope that we will be able to work out a system such as they have adopted in other countries of harvesting our crop, and still having another crop to harvest, all the while protecting the sources of water supply as they can only be protected by some measure of forest growth. We must always recognize that timber in our own western country is of special value. It is worth so much per thousand feet, but it is worth a great deal more than any actual economic value in the settlement of the country. While it is desirable that we should see that the sources of our water supplies aTe preserved it would not be possible for the government-at least I do not think it would be possible-to sit tight and say:	We will not allow this timber to be
utilized. I know that in order to meet public opinion, even if we had no other reason, we would have to provide for the utilization of the timber as it reached tne point when it was most useful as a commercial article.

Will it be your object to select only timber which has fully matured, leaving the younger timber an opportunity to grow? License holders will not be allowed to cut down acre after acre of timber, young and old.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is absolutely our policy, that is the ideal we are working to, but of course we have to meet the immediate pressure of public opinion, of the settler who wants wood and wants building logs. We are at the same time doing our best to consider the proper conservation and reproduction of the timber. I want

to assure my hon. friend that the idea he has expressed is exactly the object of our administration of the forestry branch.

That is a very old clause in the timber limits, there has been such a provision for the last 30 years, that no timber shall be taken below a certain size. How much of this area is now held under license by timber men, how much has been operated and who are the licensees in each reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As I said to the hon. member for North Toronto, I have not that information under my hand, but we have it in the department and I shall produce the figures within a day or two.
In case of a man holding a timber license in the area which you are including^ in the reserve, does he contribute anything towards the protection of his timber?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, limit holders under any circumstances, must pay a share of the cost of fire protection.
Nothing special is add-[DOT]ed for the protection when the area is taken within the park?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the limit holder does not ask to have his timber included in the forest reserve, and I do not see that we would be justified in placing him under any penalty because of our adopting this policy.

What inspection is -. qarovided^to-insure- Lhe-carrying-out-of-the regulations as to the size of timber to be cut and the protection of the reserves from fire by the removal of brush from the cutting of the timber? The regulations under which they are allowed to operate in the reserve ought to be stringent and strictly enforced.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is the intention and policy of the department, to see that the cutting of timber inside the forest reserves is done in conformity, not only with the license that has been issued', but also with our general regulations for cutting timber within forest reserves. We pay men to enforce those regulations, and if they do not do their duty they ought to be fired.

Is there any provision for replanting areas that have been cut over, or are the government simply protecting the younger trees that are left growing? More timber has been destroyed in Canada than has been used by the people, and the fires which have caused this destruction *are often caused by brush left on the ground that has been cut over. Are the government providing for the protection of this timber by having the brush removed -or destroyed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The cutting within the reserves is expected to be done under the special regulations which are applicable to the forest reserves. We liave not entered upon a policy of replanting in the areas that have been cut over. So far, we have contented ourselves with providing as well as we may for the opportunity of the younger growth to develop and for its protection. We have made some small experimental efforts in seeding and planting, but the committee will understand that with 16,000,000 acres of forest reserves, the resources of Canada are not adequate to undertake a general policy of reforestation.

This is legislation in the right direction which will have the sympathy of every member in this House. I suppose that the details of the regulations for the prevention of destruction and for reforestation will be the subject of the rules and regulations that may be made from time to time by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

When the Waterton Lakes Reserve was set apart I understood that it was the policy of the government to set apart a townsite within the reserve. Is that still the intention? Will the government survey a townsite, and by lease or in any other way give outsiders an opportunity of going in to establish a town or places of business and recreation within the limits of the reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The cash of the Waterton lakes reserve is one of the cases not provided for in the existing Act which we hope to provide for in the present Bill. The Waterton reserve is a forest reserve, the primary purpose of which is to preserve the timber growth and prevent occupation by people. Under the present Bill we propose to take power to withdraw or cut out of any forest reserve any certain area to be brought under proper regulations for occupation. Under the present Act we are not legislatively empowered to deal with the Waterton reserve ox with other like reserves as they require to be dealt with if used for purposes of recreation; but under the present Bill we shall have full authority to set apart a portion of a reserve as a place of recreation, and deal with it as may seem best. My hon. friend said something as to places of business. It may as well be Understood at the beginning that it is not proposed that these parts of reserves set apart for purposes of recreation shall be primarily places of business. There will be no business there except such as is absolutely necessary for the recreation of the people. That is the principle that is embodied in the Bill.

I wish specially to urge on the minister that provision be made for settlers to have access to a portion of the timber at all times. I refer particularly to the dry or half-dead timber. It is hard to make regulations which would be just to everybody, but I think there might be more liberal regulations with regard to that than we have had in the past. I think the minister might make provision for the removal of dry timber up to a certain size for firewood and building purposes. It would be an advantage not only to the homes of the country, but to the timber area, to have it cleared of dry timber, which is liable to cause fire and to make it spread. I would like to know what the minister proposes in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot at the present time give my hon. friend the details of our regulations; but we quite appreciate the desirability of getting rid of the dry timber. At the same time, we have to use a certain amount of care in giving people permission to enter a reserve and take timber. As between the two objects we have in view, the preservation of the good timber and the useful application of the dead timber, I want my hon. friend to understand that the Department of Forestry has quite a busy time. It is our desire to have the timber which has reached its growth, even if it is not killed by fire, but all the more if it is, utilized as freely as possible, always having regard to the proper protection of the timber generally.	[DOT]

While I would strongly recommend liberal regulations in that regard, I am aware that it is often overdone. There are many cases in which settlers unduly draw away timber without making a proper use of it, at great loss to their neighbours. So that while I would recommend liberal regulations, I would also recommend that the department see to it that those who are over-zealous do not get more than their fair share.

I am sorry to have to differ a little with my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Herron); but if such a regulation were enforced, there would be great danger of there being more dry timber to handle than there is at present. I also am in favour of giving the settlers every possible advantage, but I would rather provide for them getting green timber, for the simple reason that I think it would be hutting a premium upon unscrupulous people seeing that they always have dry timber ahead.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is one of the difficulties of the situation, and the department is very well versed in the different sides of the question. As a settler myself,
I have had to fight the government of Canada for the right to cut timber, and 11 Mr. OLIVER.	' :
have backed other people in doing so. Nobody appreciates the value to the settler of the right to cut timber for his own use, and nobody will go further to protect him in that than I will. On the other hand, the wisdom of the country, as expressed by parliament, is that the timber shall be protected, that certain laws shall be enforced, and it is my duty loyally to carry out that expressed will. I put the matter frankly before the House, and only say that the situation is very delicate and very difficult, but we bring to the discharge of the responsibility the best information we have and the best good-will both to the settler and to the wisdom of parliament in declaring the reserve.

Something has been said about reforestation. In my opinion too much is said on that subject. What this government and other governments which control timber should emphasize the most, and what they emphasize the least, is the preservation of the small timber. If the small timber of the country had the protection which it should have, until such times as the country is in a position to spend more money for reforestation than it is at present, the better it would be for the country. In many parts of the country the small timber is not marketable, bin it has probably taken fifty or seventy-five years to grow. This is the timber which should be protected, and the more we do in the line of protecting that timber and the sooner the department gets down to that basis, the sooner posterity will reap the benefit.

After this Bill passes, and a forest Teserve is set aside, what steps are to be taken to increase the park reserve in the forest reserves. On whose recommendation will that be done? Are the local governments to be consulted with reference to setting aside park reserves or game reserves? There is a reserve close to the boundary line, which, if protected, would be a great place for shooting big game, such as bears, and mountain sheep, and goats. I hope that a large portion of this forest rdserve will be set aside as a game or park reserve for that purpose. Will the local governments *be consulted?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
All forest reserves are game preserves under this Act, that is to say, so far as the jurisdiction of the Dominion government extends. It is our intention to patrol these reserves, and exercise our rights of proprietorship in the protection of game. We of course will have to come to an arrangement with the provincial governments regarding any general law concerning game, and that we hope to do as the occasion arises. As regards the setting apart of areas within the forest re-

serves as park reserves, it will not be necessary to consult any particular person or government. Whenever it appears to the department that the need exists, it will be within the rights of the department to make a recommendation to council setting apart a certain area as a park reserve and bringing it under direct regulations which will make that particular area available to the public as a pleasure resort.
On section 4,
The said reserves shall, subject to the direction of the Minister of the Interior, be under control and management of the director of forestry or such other person as is from time to time selected for that purpose by the Governor in Council.
What powers does the minister propose to give to the director? Does he propose just to work this as a department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And the director of forestry becomes simply a clerk in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. FOSTER, Is there any mutuality of advice and consultation outside of the department between the management of these reserves and the Forestry Conservation Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no direct connection. Of course all the information which the Conservation Commission collects regarding forestry work in all the provinces, and in other countries as well will be available to the forestry branch of the Interior Department just as all the information of the forestry branch is available to the Conservation Commission.
So that practically it will be under the system of patronage the same as every other department of the government. Will the Civil Service Act apply to the officers of the forestry branch?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To those who are in the city of Ottawa, of course it will, but until the Civil Service Act is made to apply to the outside service, it will not apply to those outside.
Will the hon. minister allow any further homestead entries within the bounds of these reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Will stock be allowed to graze within the areas contained in these forest reserves? Has any complaint been made to the minister personally with reference to sheep being driven into that locality under consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As set out very clearly in clause 2, there will be no homestead entries within the forest reserves. There will be no ownership, no alienation of surface rights. With regard to grazing, it is contemplated that grazing will be allowed within a forest reserve, where it is thought that such a right may be granted without prejudice to the special purpose of the growth of timber. We have not yet, however, arranged any policy in that connection. Complaints have come to my personal attention that too many sheep were being driven into the foothills for grazing, but I have also had demands from the owners of the sheep to be allowed to drive them into the foothills for that purpose. That is one of the nice little questions in the same class as the question of settlers timber, and a good many others. There are two sides to it, and each one thinks that his side is the only one. My hon. friend may be sure that the men who do not want the sheep among the foothills, and those who do, can be depended on to bring their claims and alleged rights to the attention of the Interior Department.
Under what authority are these licenses for sheep grazing granted and what regulations are proposed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not yet decided upon any regulation regarding , grazing within these park reserves. Sheep at present have no right to graze within the area covered by this Bill. Under the law certain portions of the pTairie country are set apart as sheep grazing areas, and sheep are ailowed to graze on public lands within these areas, but none of them are in the Rocky Mountain district. Any sheep grazing in the mountain or foothills are outside the protection of the law.
Is there anything in the Act to provide a certain section in which sheep can be allowed to graze?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It will be in the right of the minister or the Governor in Council to provide regulations under which, if it is thought wise, sheep may be allowed to graze within that area. As I have said, no decision has yet been reached. We do not feel that we have enough information on the subject to warrant us in formulating a policy as to grazing within that area. But once the Bill is passed, if it is passed, we will undertake, of course, to go into the matter very fully and decide what is to be done.

Is it only by order in council that certain areas may be used for sheep grazing? As I understand it there is no authority given in this Bill to allow the department to use these as sheep grazing areas. I would like to know where the minister has his contemplated authority.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In section 16, subsection (b). The word ' cattle ' is used there, but

I am under the impression that for the purposes of the law, sheep would be included under that term.

Then, I will leave the discussion of that until we come to the section referred to. I consider it very important, if the minister so understands it, that the matter should be carefully considered in this House. Speaking for myself, I have very strong objections to leaving with the minister or the Governor in Council such powers as these. It is a great liberty for the minister to exercise, to say who shall and who shall not use the public domain for his individual advantage. What I claim is that regulations of that kind should be general and every man should have an equal right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The objection of my hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve) does not lie especially against this Bill, but against all the law regarding the administration of land in all the three prairie provinces, for, at the present time, the disposition of grazing rights is a matter of regulation by the Governor in Council throughout the total area. This Bill does not change the existing conditions, but merely carries it on.

That is the reason I asked my first question, as to whether the government would have this right under the present Bill. Apparently, according to the minister, we are giving him that right. It is to guard against it that I raised the question, but, as it does not come under this clause, I will reserve further discussion on the matter.

What does the government propose to do with timber leases within the territory covered by this Bill? One method of granting these rights was what might fairly be regarded as a perpetual lease, which I think is a radically wrong principle. There was a provision in the lease to the effect that the lease should be renewable from year to year as long as there was merchantable timber standing on the tract. It is only necessary, then, for the holder of the limit to leave a few trees of merchantable timber here and there to secure a renewal of his lease. Is there any provision either in this Bill, or elsewhere that would enable the government to cancel that lease? In most of the leases it provides that if the land is needed for settlement it may be taken, but I am not sure that there is such a provision in the leases to which I have referred. If part of these areas is covered by leases of that kind, what does the government propose to do with them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I have already said, it is not the intention of the government to interfere with rights existing at the time Mr. OLIVER
of the inclusion of a certain area within a forest reserve. If a man has a homestead right, he holds it

even if he is a squatter before survey, he holds his right. And the timber-limit holder keeps his rights to his limit as if the reserve had not been created, with this difference, that under the Act, in the handling of his business on his limit he must conform to the special regulations which the government considers it desirable to enforce within the forest reserve. Otherwise, there is no interference or intention of interference with the rights held by a party before the reserve was made.

I understood that the government contemplated taking over some of these timber reserves and converting them into parks. That is what we were told in the discussion of a Bill some years ago, and I presume that there would be a similar clause in this Bill. Is it the intention of the government to take over any of these old timber reserves and keep them for park purposes, allowing no cutting of timber to go on?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have no present intention of interfering with licensees beyond the point I have mentioned-to require them to conform the conduct of their affairs on the limit to the regulations of the reserve. We do not desire to interfere with what may be called their vested rights. If we did, it would simply mean a burden upon the public treasury, which, at the present time, with so many responsibilities in connection with forest reserves we hardly think we would be warranted in imposing.

One word with reference to the point raised by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that the license holder by leaving a few trees on a limit or part of a limit could make his lease perpetual. I may say that there is also a clause which says that the department may give the licensee notice with regard to any portion of the reserve on which there is only a little timber that he must take the timber off within a specified time. This done, the government has the right to withdraw it. So, the licensee cannot retain the lease of an area on which there is practically no timber if the department does not wish him to retain it.

I remember putting the question directly when these were under consideration before, and the answer I got from the government was that as long as there was merchantable timber there they could not cancel the lease, making it practically perpetual. I think such a lease is one of the most absurd business transactions a government could perpetrate, to the injury of the people. We have example

after example in the province of Ontario of leases given thirty, forty and fifty years ago; the original leaseholders have died and the family own them still, gracti-cally holding them for ever. Timber has gone up in value six or seven times, but the royalty to the Crown is just the same as it was forty or fifty years ago. I regard it as piracy, it is little less than highway robbery of the people's property, and it is improper and wrong for any government or Governor in Council to grant leases in that way. There are leases in that country, according to the interpretation of that law by good lawyers in this House, grazing leases, held practically forever. There are timber licenses which will be held practically forever, as long as there is merchantable timber on the land. That any government should give leases of that kind is contrary to reason and common sense.
On section 5,
Is it the intention of the minister to appoint as forest rangers men having certain qualifications and technical training? This section leaves it optional with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It leaves it optional, and I do not know that we can make it any better. What is wanted is a man who knows when a fire starts and knows how to stop it. If we can get such a man, who is willing to do the best that is in him, we are doing as well as it is possible to do. The country is getting good service from such men. Our difficulty is to find such men, even without any restrictions. Under the present circumstances, the less restriction there is upon our freedom of appointment, the better men we are likely to get.

Nearly all the universities in the country have, forestry departments, and are turning ouP trained foresters. It would be a great advantage to the government to have as forest rangers men who have some knowledge and training in the science of forestry. A man may have ever so good an intention, he may be honest and all that, and yet be of little service as a firefighter because of lack of training. In certain conditions in our forests, a man requires to have a considerable amount of knowledge to be a good fire fighter.
On section 11: Act does not apply to land to which Crown has no title.

There is no provision that enables you to take this land if it has not become denuded. If the leaseholder does not see fit to take off the standing, merchantable timber, he can hold it as long as he wishes. The annual growth of timber would cover a very heavy rate of interest on the money invested, even if he held it for a hundred years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not the purpose of this Bill to interfere with existing rights. If we undertook to interfere with vested rights we would raise a great many questions which are not pertinent to the purpose in hand, and are not now to be dealt with in this Bill. We have carefully avoided raising that issue. The policy or impolicy of the granting of the original form of license is not a matter that necessarily comes into this Bill. We take the licenses as we find them and we do not interfere with the rights under them.

You take power to expropriate in several clauses.
On section 12: timber licenses.
Has the minister thought about extending that to officials in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not understand the point.
It refers to the purchase of timber, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Is not section 12 inconsistent with section 10? Section 10 says that:
The Governor in Council may secure from the holder of any title to or interest in any land within the limits of a forest reserve a waiver in writing, &c.
And section 7 as well.

Section 12 says, that the Governor in Council may not.
Neither the Governor in Council nor the minister * * is authorized * * to expropriate.
Also, as my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) points out, section 7 gives power to expropriate any land in the reserve. Standing timber is, in law, considered land, and, therefore, would come within section 10.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is in error. Section 10 is provided for the case where certain land is owned within a reserve and by reason of it being owned outside of the Crown any regulation which the Crown might make with regard to the protection of game would not apply on that particular area. It is merely to provide for the effective enforcement of any game protection that the Dominion might see fit to inaugurate within the limits of a reserve provided an arrangement can be made with the private holders, as section 10 contemplates. It might easily be that the government could not arrange with a private owner to dispose of his actual right and yet might make an arrangement to provide for a waiving of his right in so far as game protection is concerned and allow of effective protection throughout the entire reserve. This

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: has no connection whatever with the abrogation of proprietary rights. Section 12 is a provision that was inserted in the present Act at the suggestion of my hon. friends opposite who rather thought at that lime that there might be a possibility that the extraordinary powers of acquirement which are given to the Governor in Council might be used to the undue advantage of the owners of timber limits, and a provision was put in to say that the rights of limit holders should not be acquired. I hardly think that the section is necessary, but we simply preserve it in this Bill, as it was in the original. We have no objection to its being there, as we do not think it would be a wise policy to undertake to acquire these timber limits. We had not that in contemplation when we framed this Bill, and therefore, we preserved this section in the Bill.
In reference to the protection of game, does the minister contend that a private owner has the right to say we shall not protect game if we are so disposed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

If I understood him correctly, he said that provided the Governor in Council thought it desirable to protect game the carrying out of that policy is subject to the rights that a private individual possesses. How does a private person become possessed of the right to control game under a timber license or a grazing license?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are not thinking of those cases so much as of the fact that the Hudson Bay Company own two sections in every township within these forest reserves and they have not disposed of their right. They may not be willing to dispose of their right at the present time but they possibly might be'willing to waive their right with regard to the game in order that the protection that we might establish in the reserve would be efficient Otherwise, owning these sections of land, they could, in spite of this government, so long as they were in compliance with the law of the province, lease shooting rights or do anything else they pleased upon these areas, and, therefore, could set at naught our efforts for the special protection of game within these reserves.
How could the Hudson's Bay Company do that any more than a private individual could?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Any private individual who owned the title to his land, if it were included within a forest reserve, could say to us, when we undertook to make a special arrangement with him for the protection of game. I am subject to the laws of the province in regard to game, I am not subject to any guardianship of yours, I do not know you in the transaction, this Mr. OLIVER.
is my land, I treat the game on the land as my property and I will not allow you to interfere with it. We have made this provision, so that, while we would not expect possibly to make such an arrangement with a small private holder, we have thought that probably we could make such an arrangement with the Hudson Bay Company.

It appears to me to be an anomaly, that might be very awkward to handle in the future, to draw a distinction between a private owner in observing the game laws and the Hudson Bay Company, allowing one to ignore the law and compelling the other to observe it. We have regulations with regard to game in that country, have we not, under the Land Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The province legislates with regard to the protection of game. As proprietors of the land we have the right to deal with the game on that land, but we have not the right to legislate generally speaking with regard to game except upon our own land. We have no right to legislate with regard to game on another man's land.

I always thought that the laws that we had regarding game applied to all land held by the Crown as well as land held by the Hudson Bay Company. I did not understand there was any distinction; my idea was that if you made a law to protect game, it protected the game whether on a Hudson Bay lot or on a government lot, so long as the government had the constitutional right to make the law, and so with the provinces within their sphere.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Dominion has not a constitutional right to make a game law applicable to any property except what the Dominion owns. The province has a right to make a game law which applies to all land, including Dominion land, so that when parties own land within the area of a reserve in which we desire especially to protect game and exercise our rights as proprietors it is quite clear that those who have a proprietary right as against us, are not under our regulations.

You have control of all territory not coming under the control of the provinces. If in that territory you pass a law providing a close season for prairie chickens, that would apply to all land whether owned by the Hudson Bay Company or any one else.
On section 13, protection from fire along railways under construction.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: I understand the present Act applies to Dominion lands which have been erected into forest reserves. It might be wiser for this government to have a special clause in this Bill, with reference to -railways in operation, which would be different from the clause which the Minister of Railways would put in force against all the railways in the country; in other words, a railway going through a forest reserve might well be subjected to more stringent conditions in reference to fire protection than a railway in the ordinary country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Since this matter has been taken up-and the responsibility is distinctly placed upon the railway company to guard against the setting of fires, there is no greater necessity for precautions where the railway runs through a forest reserve than where it runs through valuable private property. I think that the special protection which is adequate in the one case is adequate in the other. I think it is better to leave the matter as it is in the Railway Act with the provision in this Act that is now the law in reference to railways within forest reserves. I have a further amendment which I would like to propose if the House agrees to the new section 13.
What are the provisions in the amendment to the Railway Act with reference to railways in operation through forest reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Bill is before the House and I am not absolutely familiar with its terms. The main point is that the railway companies are themselves required to pay for the patrolling of their own lines in operation.
The entire cost?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot say whether they pay the entire cost or only half the cost.
But they have to pay for the patrolling of their own line in operation, whether inside of a forest reserve or outside.

In this connection I wish to make a few remarks in regard to fires on these reserves. I think the minister will agree with me that one of the most difficult things to contend with in connection with these reserves is their protection from fire. There should be some better method of protecting them, in the interest not only of the reserves themselves, but of adjacent property. I think the minister said it was possible for the department to control the game reserves in these forest reserves. That may be, but I think it would be better for the department in that respect to work in harmony with the provincial governments, who control the game reserves. Fires are often caused on these reserves by hunters. Nearly every year the Turtle Mountain reserve is burned over. Last fall a fire started on this reserve and extended to the private property of a poor man named Balfour, of Bannerman, and destroyed everything he had, including 100 tons of hay, his house and other property. The matter is before the department; I do not know whether it has come to the notice of the minister himself or not. We had a somewhat parallel case before the House last night, in regard to a fire caused by a threshing engine. It was considered that because that fire extended beyond the limits of the Indian reserve, the government was liable for the damage done to private property, and would be willing to pay it. I think the same thing applies to this case. This man's property was destroyed from a fire which originated in the Turtle Mountain timber reserve. I ask that an investigation be made as to the origin of the fire, and the extent to which it destroyed private property, and if the minister finds that the fire originated on the property of the government, and extended to this poor man's property, he should be compensated for the damage done.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The case mentioned by my h&n. friend is hardly parallel with that which was under discussion last night. In that case the allegation was that the fire and the resulting damage was due to the carelessness of an employee of the government, and therefore, as in the case of a private individual there would be a legal responsibility, if the government had a similar responsibility it should not avoid paying the cost. In the case mentioned by my hon. friend, it is not alleged that the fire was due to the carelessness of an employee of the government. It merely started on government property. I think we had very much better go out of the forest reserve business, and go out of it quickly than to assume the responsibility for every

fire that might start on any one of these reserves. I think that would be assuming a responsibility altogether beyond the strength of the Dominion government to carry.

If these prairie reserves were fenced, and were leased for grazing purposes, I believe the danger from fire would be greatly obviated. Every year a large amount of grass grows on these reserves, and in the summer it becomes dry and forms a great fuel for fire. If cattle were allowed to graze on the reserve, it would be a benefit to the farmers, and be at the same time a great protection from fire.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That view of the case has been presented, and we hope to try it out very shortly, and I think the reserve my hon. friend mentions is one we have particularly in mind. Of course, our experiment may not be successful; it may be found that the cattle will destroy the young growth. Representations have been made to us that the grazing of the cattle would be a protection from fire, and would not injure the young growth. At any rate, we hope to try the experiment on a small scale before long.

The Railway Bill to which the minister refers does not seem to be printed yet. I have not seen the amendment, but I doubt if it extends to five miles on each side of the track; it is probable that it refers only to the right of way. While I agree with the' minister that private timber is as worthy of protection as government timber, at the same time this parliament has special interest in protecting its own timber, and these forest reserves, I understand, are especially necessary on account of the watersheds. The whole reason for setting t.he Rocky Mountain park on the eastern slope aside as a forest reserve is to protect the rivers of the hon. minister's own province, so that this parliament has a special interest in protecting the timber in that section. It would be a national disaster if that timber should be burnt. Even if the railway companies are to pay compensation in case of damages, that would by no means make up for the national loss should there be a big fire. While this section provides for taking care of the timber, and while the railways are to provide certain protection for five miles on either side of the track, my impression is that the Railway Act will not go that far. I submit to the minister, if he wants to keep the timber on the eastern slope of the Rockies, that it would be better to have some special provision more stringent and extending a greater distance from the railway than the Minister of Railways probably thinks advisable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am under the impression that when we have laid upon the rail-Mr. OLIVER.
way companies, as the Minister of Railways proposes, the burden of patrolling all I their lines in operation, we are asking as much as is fair from them, and it is for us to take efficient measures for the protection of the property of the Crown at the distance my hon. friend suggests. We only propose this measure not knowing what is to be included in the Railway Act. I desire that the railway companies shall bear a fair share of the burden of fire protection because certainly they are the most incorrigible and persistent fire setters, but I do not wish to be unfair to them. We lay the burden upon the railway corporations very strongly under this Bill during construction. Then during operation, I think that the Board of Railway Commissioners is really the proper authority to have control, and I would prefer to leave the matter in that way for the present. I propose, however, to add another clause to read as follows:
Every fire-ranger appointed to patrol a line of railway under construction or in operation shall be furnished by the person constructing or operating such railway with free transportation on all trains running on such railway, whether passenger, freight or con* struction trains, while in the discharge of his duty.
So thus we shall take that advantage of the railways by compelling them to transport free our men engaged in the fire protection service.

I am not desirous in any way of imposing heavier burdens on the railway companies. I had no intention of claiming that the railway companies should pay a larger share than the minister is providing in this Bill, but what I was concerned about is the efficiency of the protection. I thought that since we have not the proposed clause in the Railway Act before us, it would be wise to go a little slowly until we find out whether the Minister of Railways is providing in his Bill as efficient protection to the national parks as this measure proposes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When we ask from the railways the same protection in the parks that we ask everywhere else, we ask as much as we should, and it will be for the forestry branch of the Interior Department to see that, over and above that, efficient protection is given. If, after this new provision of the Railway Act comes into operation, we still find that the railway companies are not bearing their fair share of the expense, it will be quite in order to make a further change. But I think we are going as far as we are warranted now if the House will adopt the further provision which I have just moved, and which will compel the railways to give our patrolmen free transportation.

If this clause should pass, would it include only the officer in charge of the fire-patrol or also the men fighting the fire? For instance a number of men might be brought for a distance of ten or twenty miles to fight the fire.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This will apply to every one employed. ' Every fire-ranger appointed to patrol.'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The following amendment is proposed:
Every fire-ranger appointed to patrol a line of railway under construction or in operation shall be furnished by the person constructing or operating such a railway with free transportation on all trains running on said railways, whether passenger, freight or construction trains, while in the discharge of his duties.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Call that section 14, and then renumber all the others.
Would a settler, for instance, who was ordered out to fight a fire, be an officer in the sense meant by the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid he would not.
I would not like again, when introducing a new principle such as this, to carry it too far. If we do not find the clause sufficient, we can go further another time. We are making a long step in advance in this Bill, and the . Railway Act over what we have had before.

Does not that give an inspector very large powers of travel over a railway?_ He might travel-on the-Canadian Pacific railway from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and say he was in the discharge of his duties. Should not this free transport be limited to within the confines of the reserve of which he is inspector?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This section does not apply merely to the reserve, but to anywhere in the Dominion where there are fires to combat.
Would a ranger appointed in British Columbia have the right to go down to Manitoba to look after a fire there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would think not. I think that the words ' in the discharge of his duties ' place a sufficient limit. That means within the limits of his patrol.
I should think it would be better to say ' within the limits of his jurisdiction.'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would be all right. Mr. Chairman, will you make the change suggested by the hon. member (Mr. Middle-bro)?
Suppose the railway was not one under federal charter, but under provincial charter?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am under the impression that this section would apply just the same.
I am very well satisfied that it ought to; and, so far as this parliament has jurisdiction, it will. I think this parliament has sufficient jurisdiction, but, if it has not, we cannot do better than adopt this provision, anyway.

When members of parliament and senators were given the right to travel on railways, it was held that this parliament could only give that right so far as railways under federal jurisdiction were concerned. Will you be able to go further in the case of a fire ranger than you did in the case of a member of parliament? Here are two provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, each of which has power to charter railways. They are building railways through federal property. Fire rangers would be employed along these railways to prevent fire. If we have not the right to give authority to a member of parliament to travel on a provincial railway, would we have that right to give authority in this other case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think that, all things considered, and it being a case in which it is conceded that private and public property is being protected from these very railways,
I think that in the public interest we should assume that we have the power.

I would rather hear the opinion of some eminent lawyer on that subject, for it seems to me if we have not the right in one instance we have not it in the other. It does not depend upon a question of protecting property, constitution-, ally we have the right or we have not the right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not quite see the point the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule), makes. If we have not this right, we do not need to say we have not it; but by declaring it, if we have it, it becomes effective, I think it will not be wise to enact any exception to this provision; I do not think it is called8'for.

What I contend is this: When we were dealing with the question of members of this House and of the Senate travelling on railways, I think, it was agreed that we had not the power to deal with provincial railways. If we have control for that purpose, it seems to me we cannot possibly have the right of control for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not learned in the law, any more than my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule), but I think the two purposes are radically different. In the case of the transportation of members of parliament, the railway could not be assumed to have any direct interest or responsibility, whereas

in the case of the protection of property from fire, the railway has a direct interest and responsibility. And it seems to me, that the conditions being as they are, our business is to say that they shall carry these fire-rangers, and it is for them to say they will not if they do not wish to.
It might be all right in equity, but in law I think both cases would be the same.

If we pass this legislation and a locally chartered railway wishes for free right of way across the Dominion forest . reserve, it must apply to the minister, who could make it conditional that they shall comply with this law.

That would be all right, but it would be done by negotiation.
- Mr. PERLEY. Yes, when we pass the legislation it may be. made^applicable to them by negotiation, whereas, if this were not in the Bill, the minister might not have the necessary power.

I think that as to railways actually constructed under provincial charter, we should not have the right to impose conditions on them. But in the case of a provincially chartered railway wanting to go through the reserve, it could be made a condition that they shall comply with the Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The proposed section reads:
Every fire-ranger appointed to patrol along the line of a railway under construction or in operation shall be furnished by the person constructing or operating such railway with free transportation on all trains running on such railway through the district for which he is appointed and while in the discharge of his duty, whether they are passenger, freight or construction trains.

Arc there any mounted policemen attached to the Interior Department and looking over the forest reserves?
I believe that was a case in years gone by?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 14,
Under this clause will any person be prohibited from carrying arms within a reserve? Are the regulations in this clause going to govern the carrying of arms?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These are not regulations; the regulations will be made by the Governor in Council from time to time. This is a measure for the enforcement of the regulations.

In reference to subsection 3, will the forest ranger have a right to Mr. OLIVER.
search any house in the reserve without a wr arrant?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a question how far we are warranted in carrying the jurisdiction of these forest rangers. If we are going to take efficient measures for the protection of the game, we must have some authority outside the limits of the reserve. Perhaps ten miles is too far, I am not going to insist upon that, but they should be allowed some jurisdiction outside the boundaries of the reserve if there is to be efficient protection of the game.
How does the minister arrive at the distance within which he can search for arms? If you are going outside the reserve at all, you must have some reason for stopping within the prescribed distance.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give any reason why we should either go as far as ten miles, or less. This is an arbitrary right which we consider necessary for efficient protection of the game, and when we are giving such an arbitrary right we should not extend it to any great distance. It is a matter of opinion whether the distance should be limited to ten miles, or five miles, or whether it should exist at all.
If the Hudson Bay Company sells their land, it will be to provide owners, and how are you going to deal with those people to prevent them from having a gun?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have in a previous section of the Bill taken , authority to purchase, or even to expropriate, 'such rights within the reservation, either to acquire them by purchase, by exchange or by expropriation. Already under the Act of 1896 in relation to these reservations, we have spent a considerable amount of money in buying out the rights of settlers, homesteaders and even squatters, for the reason that we must have the ownership of the land in order that we may exercise proper jurisdiction for the protection of game. In regard to the Hudson Bay Company, they have not disposed of any of their lands within the reserve. Since we passed the Act of 1896 they have retained their land, and they are in negotiation with the government on the subject of an exchange of that land, but so far we have not yet reached a conclusion. It is hoped that later on we will be able to make a fair exchange with the Hudson Bay Company, so that their right's within the reservation will pass entirely to us.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The instructions are to secure his removal by mild means if possible, and if not possible, to take legal proceedings to eject him. So far we have not had to take such proceedings very often, because when people find that they must go they go without being forced. But that is one of the many features of the administration of this law that is anything but pleasant.

I can understand that. The reason I ask is that I have known good provincial laws placed on the statute-book under which no man had a right to squat on Crown lands, but it was broken every day because there was no enforcement of the law to prevent squatting.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If my hon. friend had been here in previous sessions, or at a previous time, he would have heard some strong complaints as to the action taken by the department in this respect. My apology at that time was that we were instructed by parliament to clear the reserve, and we had to cleaT it.
Those references were to squatters that were previously on the land, were they not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Squatters who had gone on the land after the reservation had been declared. The reservation was declared by departmental order, and squatters came on even after that departmental order had been given, and they had to be disposed of.

In what-position will the federal authority be, provided a provincial authority pass game laws in conflict with those of the federal authority? A good deal of this land will be in the provinoe of Alberta, which has a right to pass its own game laws. What will happen if there is a conflict of authority between the province and the Dominion in regard to game laws?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think not. The. whole purpose in setting apart this reserve, in so far as game is concerned, is to preserve the game. Therefore, any law of the province that contemplates the prevention of the killing of game at some time or other will be acceptable to the Dominion, in this way, that the Dominion will not be anxious to issue authority to kill game at a time when the province says it shall not be killed. There will be no conflict between the two authorities in that way. The only difference will be that under our law there may be greater restrictions against the killing of game than there would be under the provincial law. We will operate within the provincial law and therefore, there will be no conflict. If we undertook to operate outside of the provincial law and authorized the killing of game when the provincial law said it should not be killed there would be a conflict, but so long as we keep within the provincial law and not only say that game shall not be killed, when the province says it shall not be killed, tout that it shall not be killed at other times, there can be no danger of a conflict.

There might be conflict if the provincial law should set aside as a time for the killing of game the time that you say shall be a close season. The question that naturally arises is, who has the authority to pass the game laws? It i3 admitted that the province has. To assume that the game laws will be exactly the same always will toe assuming something that is not likely to happen. It seems to me that there would toe very great chances of a conflict of authority.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The two townships mentioned were included in the first reserve made by departmental order about 1900. They have been under reservation ever since, and the objections that have been urged against the reservation are the objections which are to be urged against every forest reserve that is established anywhere in the Dominion. The man or settlement established next a reserve does not want the reserve there for obvious reasons. I am glad my hon. friend has brought this matter up because that is a side of the question that does not strike the average

member of parliament; but, the member who has a reserve in his constituency understands that each forest reserve is necessarily a cause of irritation to the settlers immediately adjacent to the reserve. Under all the circumstances I cannot hold out any prospect of the withdrawal of the two townships mentioned.
In regard to the small corner of one township where the Canadian Northern enters the reserve, we had the inspection made to which my hon. friend alludes and to which the settlers in the vicinity object. The inspector is as positive in his view as the settlers are in their view, and it seems to me, in view of the very positive representations made by the inspector, that we would not be warranted in asking parliament to withdraw the sections at this time. I had hoped that this Bill would have been passed during the winter and so assumed that it would not be possible to have a second inspection of the ground made after the snow was off the ground; otherwise I should have had a second inspection made. Under the circumstances I did not see that I could do anything but accept the representations of the inspector. I think it is an unsafe principle to adopt that when we have set aside reserves by Act of parliament, have spent large amounts in securing the removal of people from the reserves, have held out to all the world that they are going to be reserves, we should then undertake to throw them open unless there is a very well established case.

Apart from the general objection of settlers in a district to the establishment of a forest reserve near them, there is in this case that very strong objection on the part of the municipality from a municipal standpoint. It is a serious thing for a municipality to be cut in two and not have any settlement between the two sections of it; it causes all taxes for schools, roads and bridges to fall upon a smaller number of people than would otherwise be the case, and, therefore, they cannot secure the improvements they would desire. I would urge this objection more strongly from the municipal standpoint than from the individual standpoint. What is the name of the inspector who made the inspection?
