The minister has stated the difficulty that he has found in dealing with persons who desire special privileges; and yet by this subsection he is asking for an unlimited, arbitrary and extremely valuable power. This section names privileges, which I do not hesitate to say would run up to millions of dollars in value, which it is proposed to place arbitrarily in the hands of the minister. If this Bill passes he becomes an absolute czar in regard to the granting of these privileges. I do not think this parliament should place any man in that position. In the past such absolute power in the hands of a minister has led to a great deal of trouble, and many instances have occurred in which its exercise has been very much to the injury of the public domain. Private individuals have been able to make large gains, in some cases immense fortunes, in cases exactly parallel, to this. Hon. gentlemen know that some years ago there were scandals in regard to leases granted to certain men in the western provinces. Yet by this Bill we are placing in the hands of one man the sole authority to grant similar privileges, One man might go to the minister, and ask for the special privilege of grazing sheep or cattle, and might apparently make out a good case for it. Another man who came afterwards might have an equal right, but in the mind of the minister might not make out an equally good case, and be refused. I say this power is a dangerous power to place in the hands of any man. I think the minister should first submit to parliament the regulations which he proposes to apply to these matters, and they should be such that all men would be placed on an equal basis.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What the hon. member has said is absolutely true. But the responsibility supposed to be assumed here by the Governor in Council and laid on the shoulders of the minister is exactly the responsibility he has now, and for my part, I do not know any other way of handling the business under the circumstances. All these matters mentioned in subsection (b) of section 16 are now under the same control, throughout the three prairie provinces, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon

Territory, and always have been. So that the condition is not new. It is a condition which has prevailed for many years. The particular objection to providing by statute for each of these matters mentioned in subsection (b) is that we are undertaking the administration of a new responsibility for a purpose which is only in embryo in the public mind, which has not yet been worked out to a detailed conclusion.
We do not know yet how best we can carry on the business in these several parts bo as to get the best result. We have to provide to use the timber and at the same time provide for the protection and reproduction of the timber. Then we have to provide for the mineral development and make that provision under such restrictions as will still protect the timber. We must also make provision that the public shall not have the free right of ingress and egress, but that, under certain restrictions, they shall have the enjoyment of these parks. I need not say more to show that in dealing with a new condition, we cannot be expected to provide legislation which will prove in every respect satisfactory; -and under the circumstances, it is much better to administer by order in council so that regulations may be adopted from time to time as the conditions change and our information increases.

speechtext:
If there were no other reason against this Bill than the fact that the provincial government sent its representative here to remonstrate with the federal government as to the unwisdom of passing this measure, that is a sufficiently strong reason why we should refuse to pass it. I do not think we should always endeavour to place ourselves in antagonism to the provincial governments. Those governments, I think, are properly believed to have prior rights in this country. They were in existence before the federal government was formed. They gave up a part of their rights to permit the federal government to be formed, but others they maintained for their own purposes, and one of these is the right to grant authority by incorporation of a company to build railways within their own boundaries. It was in pursuance of that right that the provincial government opposed this Bill, because the railway it proposes to charter is in reality only a provincial railway, and what is tacked on to it is tacked on simply to bring it within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. I can see no other reason for it. Now, I think it is our duty to examine these proposals very carefully when they are submitted to us, and bring our judgment to bear on the question as to whether or not they are an interference with provincial railway, and what is tacked on to avoid such interference as far as possible; and when we have not only the circumstances surrounding this proposed railway to1 indicate that it is a provincial railway, but the fact that the provincial government sent its representative here to remonstrate against it, saying that it would he injurious to.the province's system of railways and to its aim, we should be very slow to encroach on the domain of the province in that respect. Now, this railway has a main line and two branches. All railways are expected to build their main line first. The branches of this railway could never be successfully operated in connection with it, if they were ever intended to be operated with it, until the main line were built. The proposal of my hon. friend from Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) is that the company shall build the main line to the point where the branches branch off, and

then build the branches. If they build the main line, which is within federal jurisdiction, that would be an evidence that they had a bona fide purpose in coming here for the charter. But the proposed railway, I contend, is only a device to circumvent the rights of the province-to get the right under a federal charter to build a railway in the province which should be built under a provincial charter if it is built at all. I do not think we should support that device or play into their hands. It seems to me that we should have sufficient respect for the province to give it fair play in the situation. The province has inaugurated its own railway policy and system. Why was the Timiskaming and Northern railway carried away back into the wilds of that country? It was done for two or three purposes:	First, to open
up the country for settlement, and, secondly, to supply the needs of the country in connection with the opening up of new mines. Since the Cobalt mines- were found in that country, the provincial government has exerted itself to its utmost to- give the people railway facilities. It has now its railway in operation. It goes into a country where there is not a very good supply of railway traffic to support a railway, and unless it has feeders it must be a financial failure to the province. When a province undertakes to build its own railway system, it should not make the same fatal mistake and blunder that the federal government did, when it built the Intercolonial railway as a main trunk line and failed to provide feeders for it in the shape of branch lines. The province, desiring to profit by the mistakes of the federal government in this respect, -when they mapped out their railway system in these northern wilds, made up their minds to throw out a branch line whenever a new mine was opened up or a new settlement took place. They are doing that at very great expense to the province, and some of these branches may not pay for a long time to come. But there is no locality in that country suffering badly for the need of a railway, and, therefore, there is no strong argument why another railway should come in and share with the provincially-owned railway in the traffic of that country. They want to have a paying railway at as early a date as possible, and, therefore, do not look with unconcern on any company or any other scheme that is calculated to take away the traffic that rightly belongs to that railway. What is here proposed? This railway has three lines. At first it starts from the Transcontinental railway at a point in the province of Quebec in order to bring it under the federal parliament. Then it goes across the boundary line into Ontario, and then starts its branch line from the Northern Ontario railway, a government-owned railway, to take away the freight that properly belongs to that road. The Ontario government are prepared to build a line into this locality just as soon as a railway is needed there. Why then grant a charter to any company for the purpose of building a branch line which will take away from the traffic of a provincial-owned railway? That is unjust to the province.
The hour for Private Bills having expired the committee rose and reported progress.

speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill (No. 85) respecting Forest Reserves and Paras -Mr. Oliver.
On section 16,

When the House rose at six o'clock I was very glad to hear the Minister of the Interior agree with me regarding the great responsibility which wili devolve upon him in this connection, and also with regard to the immense value of the natural resources of which this measure will give him the absolute control. He said that he agreed in every particular with the remarks I made, but gave as _ a reason for having this section in the Bill the fact that the administration of these resources has been carried on in a .similar manner by this government before, and that there was great difficulty in making general regulations which would restrict and control the giving away of these vaci-ous resources. It does not appeal to me as a sound reason that because this government allowed certain things to occur previously they should continue that policy. If that policy has been shown to be injurious to the public interest, and to have resulted in abuses, we ought to endeavour to change it, and prevent this abuse in the future. That is why I should like to see this particular clause cut out.	_
This clause Tefers, amongst other things, to mineral deposits. The hon. minister will remember that the Dominion Mining Institute has for years taken special exception to the administration by the Department of the Interior of mineral deposits ;n the lands under its control. So strongly do they feel on this point that there has not been a year, when it has not been brought up at their annual meeting. They have appealed to the Mines Department to bring in a Bill setting forth fixed regulations governing the disposal of minerals on Dominion government lands. We had that question- up in the Mines Committee, of which the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) is chairman, but I regret that so far that committee has not brought in a Bill dealing with this matter. I remember one instance cited by the Dominion Mining Institute. Certain capitalists had

sent out prospectors into that northern country, and had them there two years at heavy expense. These inspectors found certain indications of value, and the parties made application to the Interior Department, but after considerable delay they were informed that they could not obtain the mining rights. They withdrew in disgust their prospectors, and said that under such conditions no man would undertake to prospect in that country. I give that simply as an illustration. The same thing has occurred with regard to the cutting of timber. I cannot see why this government should not have fixed general regulations for the disposal of timber in these park reserves. Let them regulate the manner of cutting so as to save the young trees, and let them throw open the cutting of the timber to public auction, and give every one a fair chance. Let them give the cutting of the timber to the men who comply with the regulations, and whose tenders are the highest. In that way the feeling that there is undue favouritism would be removed, the department would be relieved of much responsibility, and the public would have greater confidence in the administration of these reserves. Without going further into this argument, I think the minister will see the force of some regulation of that nature being imposed before we give him the absolute control of resources of such great value.
This Bill also deals with water-power sites and power transmission. A few years ago these things were considered of not much value, not only in Canada, but in most places; but to-day the use of electrical energy from water-power has made such advances that it is probably one of the most valuable of our resources. We can readily understand therefore how men will endeavour to get control of the water-powers which are on these reserves. The main argument made for this reserve on the eastern slope of the Rockies' is that it controls the headwaters of the magnificent rivers and 1 other water-powers we have there, so that any one will see that the clause ,we are now considering is dealing with resources of immense value. And one should not have to emphasize the necessity of our having a standard set of regulations governing them, so that applicants for water rights would know the exact conditions under which they could obtain them, the rates fixed, the length of time they could have the use of them, &c. It is not a sufficient answer for the minister to say that it is difficult to make sdch regulations. We are here to discharge our duties and responsibilities, no matter how difficult, and see that the public is protected. We know what our own commission appointed by this government has said regarding these water-powers, and the neces-Mr. GOODEVE.
sity of protecting them. I submit that we should not pass_ this clause as it stands, but that the minister should be prepared to give this parliament some idea of what regulations he proposes to adopt in the disposing of these various natural resources mentioned in this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that I can add anything to what I said before the House rose at six o'clock. I said then that the whole of the provisions of the subsection to which my hon. friend alludes are already in force under the same jurisdiction, and are applied to the whole of the territory that is under federal control. We are not asking for something in this Bill that is not already conferred upon and exercised by the same authority that is alluded to in the Bill. If my hon. friend thinks that what has been practicable during the last fifteen or twenty years in regard to the whole country is not applicable to this small section of it, then of course he may call for legislation in regard to that particular part. But as I said before, the fact that we are undertaking to work out a theory and a policy in regard to forest and water conservation, dealing with a matter which is as yet in embryo, and which must be worked out according to experience gained-I say under those circumstances his demand that there should be cast into legislative form all the various regulations that are required in the administration of the resources mentioned under this section, is scarcely a reasonable one, and is not one that he would consider reasonable if he were in my position. As to the water-power regulations, my hon. friend is surely aware that all water-powers under the control of the Dominion government are subject to well defined regulations, which are admitted by all who have studied them to have conserved the public interest on the one hand and the development of power on the other, and which are generally admitted to be more satisfactory than anything else that has been attempted in any country in the world. I do not think under these circumstances we are asking too much in asking that the same authority under which all these natural resources are administered throughout the Northwest Territories and the Yukon should be exercised on this reservation.

This is a more important provision than appears at first sight. The Bill covers an area of 16.000,000 acres of land, Dominion lands, grazing lands and mineral lands, and I have no doubt that the minister is given power under this section to dispose of timber, minerals and other resources representing a value of perhaps four or five hundred million dollars. So we are giving to the Governor in Council, which of course means the government, the absolute power to dis-

pose in such manner as they see fit of the assets of this country worth four or five hundred million dollars. Now it is an admitted principle that parliament should have control over its own assets, and that the most democratic form of government is that which submits to parliament the proposed disposition of the country's assets. Under the proposed section I conceive that the minister would have the right for instance to dispose of all the gold, silver, copper and other minerals, on these nine reserves in the province of British Columbia. In addition to that, the minister would have the right to make leases for any length of time he should deem proper of all the timber limits contained on this reserve, also of all grazing rights for cattle and other animals. In the province of Manitoba there are five reserves where there are valuable timber and grazing rights, and probably mineral rights; in Saskatchewan six reserves, and in Alberta four reserves, 24 reserves altogether, containing some 16,000,000 acres of land. Now that gives to the Governor in Council, and to the Minister of the Interior particularly, very large powers. I should think that the minister would like to protect himself against the encroachments of some of his whilom friends, and in order to do that, I should think he w;ould desire some uniform standard regulations with regard to each proposed concession; just for instance, as we have a model clause when we are granting charters to railway companies, and a model clause when we are - granting charters to telephone companies. There are model clauses to which every proposed company seeking incorporation has to submit. In the same way I think the minister could put a provision of that kind in the proposed section 16. If you do that, then, if you are going to offer a mineral lease, if you are going to offer a concession for sale, all you have to say to the purchaser is: Here are the rules and regulations we have made with respect to mineral rights or mineral leases for this reserve; we are going to put that up for sale bv auction on a certain day, you will have the same right to tender as any one else. After being duly advertised for sale the inference is that the government will get a fair price for the concession. The same rule will apply to all other concessions put up by the minister, because the minister admits that this section gives him the power to make regulations, and it is admitted that he will make regulations. Now if he does that with regard to each concession, why not go a step further and say that the sale of this concession under this regulation shall be by public auction, so that the public may have a right to tender. I see no objection to that, and for that purpose I propose that the following
amendment be inserted at the end of subsection (c):
Provided that prior to the exercise of any of the powers in this subsection contained, a uniform standard giving the conditions and terms of sale for each class of concession shall be imposed, and that the intention to dispose of such concession shall be duly advertised, and such concession shall be sold by public auction under such standard conditions and terms.
There is another section of the Act which says that the regulations which are to be made under this must be submitted to parliament. So in this way we will get the regulations submitted to parliament and approved, and then we will have standard written uniform regulations that he who runs may read. Every man who proposes to buy a concession will know the exact conditions of sale, and when you put a concession up by public auction, with all the conditions attached to it, it will be sold to the highest bidder. I do not think you can apply any more just or reasonable principle to the sale of the assets of the country, or one that will better assure to the public the highest price of the asset you intend to sell. I ask the minister in all earnestness to allow me to make this amendment. I would point out that the principle is adopted so far as the regulations are concerned. These regulations are to be submitted to parliament, and the minister should go one step further and adopt the principle of sale by public auction, and this amendment will carry out that provision.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve), and my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), seem not to be exactly at one in their consideration of this section. My hon. friend from Kootenay states that there should be legislative provision covering . the disposition of the rights to these several natural resources. My hon. friend from North Grey is willing that these should be disposed of by regulation, but the regulation must provide that they shall be disposed of by auction. My hon. friend from North Grey seems to be under the impression that we have not any regulation, that he who runs may read, under which our natural resources are disposed of.

The minister has misunderstood me. I have read the old Act, and I knew that there were regulations. But thev are not specific as under this Act. You have no Act which says that the concession must be sold by public auction. But we have that principle in connection with our public works-where the amount involved is beyond a certain amount there must be public advertisement and tender. Why should the same principle not hold

when selling assets worth millions and millions of dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That only shows hlow difficult it is to understand something that a man is not familiar with. There are certain natural resources, the rights to which it is perfectly feasible and proper to dispose of by public auction. But there are certain other natural resources, the rights to which should not be disposed of by public auction.
Can the minister give us an instance of each?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, that is what I propose to do. We do dispose now of rights to timber by public auction-that is what our regulations provide for. So far as that is concerned the rights of the public, and also of the individual who undertakes to utilize these materials are conserved. That is *considered to be in the public interest. But when it is a matter of disposing of mineral rights, I think the hon. gentleman will search the world in vain for a case in which mineral rights are disposed of by public auction.
Why, the Ontario government sold a mineral right by public auction, and received a million and a quarter for it.
And it was given away by that government's predecessors.	i

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can only say that in my humble judgment the way to deal with mineral rights is the same as to deal with land rights, and that is to give them away.
I think that is sound public policy.
That is the way they used to do in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am here to say, and to argue the point if necessary, that the best way in the public interest to dispose of mineral rights-speaking of rights to precious metals-is to give them away. And that is the way to dispose of public lands- to give the land away. I do not know that we need discuss the reasons for that. But, just as my hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro), holds one view, I hold the other, and, judging by the lines of administration which prevail throughout the world, my view is favoured by the majority. Now, with regard to water-power rights, in my humble judgment it would not be wise in the public interest to dispose of them by auction sale. The advantage to the public in connection with water-power rights is in the abundance and cheapness of the power that can be produced.
But cannot the hon. gentleman attain that object by regulating rates? Put on a stringent regulation if you like and then offer the concession for sale Mr. MIDDLEBRO.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under the regulations we have, provision is made for regulating rates at which power shall be sold, and there is also provision for regulating the rental that shall be paid by the lessee for the use of the power. It must be obvious that,if that right is sold by public auction and a sum of money is paid by the lessee for the right, the ultimate user of the right is the man who must pay that money. What I judge to be the great benefit of the utilization of power is the quantity that can be produced and the cheapness with which it can be supplied, and, just in proportion as you charge a price for the right to produce that power, you lay an additional tax upon the consumer. In my humble judgment, that is not sound public policy. I am quite aware that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Middlebro) has as good a right to his opinion as I have to mine. He represents one view, the national treasury, while I represent the other view, the public interest.
I am representing the view of getting rid of political favouritism by putting these rights up to public competition.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as that is concerned, the hon. gentleman will find that, under the regulations of other countries than Ontario there is no room for political favouritism if the regulations are administered as they should be. And that there are regulations for the disposal of water-powers where there is equally no room for political favouritism. The question of political favouritism is not necessarily settled by an auction sale, nor does it necessarily appear when an auction sale does not take place. I am willing to accept the principle of auction sale when that principle is in the public interest, but, from my point of view, it is not wise to accept the principle of auction sale in the matter of mineral rights or water-power rights, or, for that matter grazing rights.

Does not the hon. minister see that there is a great difference between a mine and a farm? Does not he see that it is in the public interest that the farm should be settled, because you thereby increase the productiveness of the land and add to your population? But to give away mineral rights, as the minister suggests, for nothing, though they may be. worth two or three millions-surely he must see that it would be better, in the public interest, to secure the two or three milion for the benefit of the treasury rather than leave it in the hands of private individuals. For that is what it means when the minister says he would give away a mineral right rather than sell it. In other words, he would sooner give a couple of million dollars into the hands of-I will not say a friend, but a private individual-instead of securing it

for the public interest. I certainly differ from the minister on that point. There is a clear distinction between farming land and a mine. In the case of a water-power, in spite of what the hon. minister says, he can make regulations as stringent as he likes in the public interest, and then sell a concession to the highest bidder.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But the price he will give will have to come out of the consumer just the same.
But if you give it to the lessee for nothing, what is the advantage?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But it is on the principle of regulating the rates at which power may be sold, thus bringing the price down to the lowest possible point. And everybody knows that on cheap power the prosperity of industry in which machinery is used depends.

In one case you rely upon him to whom you give it to bring the price to the lowest possible point, but in the other case vou make the regulations as severe as you choose in the interest of the public and sell it by public auction. You know then whether you are getting just what it is worth or not.

It struck me that the argument of the minister in justification of this clause was a very weak one. He says we have this principle in the Land Act, that we have been administering public rights under that law and we are only going a little further, but doing the-same thing. Let him ask himself for a moment what has been our experience under what he is pleased to call the correct principle? Did it turn out good or bad? Look at the administration of the timber berths in the country. What has that been? We have had the greatest public scandals ever perpetrated in Canada, absolute piracy, dishonesty, thievery, fraud and what belonged to the whole people was converted to the use of a few individuals improperly and dishonestly, under the very low and the very principle that he is defending to-night. In my judgment our experience of the past is the strongest argument possible why we should devise some other means for dealing with these matters in future because that which has been pursued in the past has not been a success. It has been admittedly a failure, and that is known from one end of Canada to the other.
There is another reason why I think there is a good deal of force in the argument of my hon. friend from North Grey. What we are dealing with is not our own. It belongs to the people. What are the government? They are the trustees for the time being, handling the assets of the people, and like every other trustee who is dealing with something in the nature of a trust they are hound to make the very best
possible use of the asset that they can in order to give the largest return to the owners. Are they doing that by this system? Are they doing it when they are acting in this way? The hon. gentleman says that he would give away a mine as well a3 he would give away land. Suppose that by an accident of Providence, or whatever you like to call it, there is great wealth stored away in small compass in the ground; it belongs to the Dominion of Canada and the Minister of the Interior is the party who is entrusted with the duty of seeing that it is administered in such a way as to bring to the owners the largest return. Yet he says that he would give it away. That is not getting the largest return from it. The party who works it is entitled to a reasonable profit out of his labour and out of the money invested in it, but the return to him is likely to be more than a dozen profits on his operations. Who is entitled to the return over and above what is a reasonable profit? Are not the owners entitled to that- the people of Canada? Therefore I say that when it is handled in trust it should be the duty of theTtrustees to handle it so as to get the largest returns for the owners, and when they are doing that, in my judgment they are doing what is good business, and they are following out a principle that is universally admitted to be the proper principle for every trustee to be guided by in administering a trust. The minister said something with reference to mines. He believed in giving them away. When I can get the attention of the minister with all the many attractions elsewhere, I will address myself to the subject. When a minister is in charge of a Bill and a member is endeavouring to criticise the measure, and is addressing himself to the subject, he is entitled to receive the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I wish to apologize to the hon. gentleman by saying that I was asking my hon. friend (Mr. Nesbitt) on my right-
You have no right to ask a question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was asking my hon. friend on my right a question to bring to my mind a point that my hon. friend was speaking on at the moment. It was not any lack of attention to what he was saying, but I was wishing to keep myself informed as to the thread of the hon. gentleman's discourse.
If that is the explanation I will exonerate the hon. gentleman from any desire to he discourteous, but I thought that I saw him trying to attract the attention of other hon. gentlemen around him.
I take the opportunity of endorsing what the hon. minister has said.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend is too suspicious.

I do not know that the endorsement comes with very good grace from the hon. gentleman. I was just trying to give an example of the two systems. The late Sir Oliver M-owat and his successor, Mr. Ross, seemed to have the same idea with regard to the administration of a trust that the Minister of the Interior has to-night, and in pursuance of that they took the mines of Ontario and absolutely gave them away to their own friends.
No, no.

I say yes; and the history of it is so plainly written on every page of the late government's record, that he who runs may read, if he were only half blind, and then he would not be any worse than the hon. member for Huron when it comes home to him. What was the result? They were harrowing money to carry on the affairs of the government of the province, they were squandering the assets of the province, and when the change oE government was made it was found that they had given away four-fifths of the valuable mines in Ontario. Mr. Chairman, I would like to have order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman has good order.

When I hear men talking in ordinary conversational style I hardly think it is good order. I was saying that they had given away nearly four-fifths of the valuable mines when the present government came in. What did they do? They took a small portion of a lake, they took remnants, they took mines here and there, endeavoured to find out the value of these mines, advertised them for sale and they got as high a value as they could for them. What did they bring back to the people of the province of Ontario between the time that the preceding government went out and they came into power-a period of about seven years? There has been derived from these mines between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000. That belongs to the province of Ontario, whereas, similar resources were being squandered by the predecessors of the present government. This result has been accomplished by virtue of a change in policy that recognized it to be the duty of trustees to use the trust confided to their care to bring back the largest return to the owners. What are they doing to-day? One of those mines alone is bringing over $70,000 a year that was not bringing $100 a year when the present government came into power. This revenue Was being given away and the same principle Mr. SPROULE.
obtained with regard to nearly all the valuable mines in Ontario. To-day the province is getting a large return from them and the result is that although the government are spending more in the interest of the people of the province they are still able to carry on the affairs of the province with great success, and they are doing it greatly to the benefit of the people. They are doing that by virtue of a different method of administering the trust confided to them than that proposed by the Minister of the Interior, and it should be a strong argument in favour of the wisdom of trying to handle that which is given to you in trust in such a way that it brings the largest returns to the owners for whom that trust is being administered.
By carrying it out in this way you are not likely^ to do that. Our experience in the past is the best evidence of this, and I know of no better criterion by which to judge the future than the experience of the past. What has been the experience of the past under the law the minister is defending to-night? It has been one of wasteful extravagance and dishonesty. I am free to admit that under regulations properly carried out in the spirit and letter we might get a much better return than we have got in the past under many regulations. Not only was the law bad because it was on a wrong principle, but the regulations were not properly enforced, and the result was great loss to the Dominion of Canada in the administration of timber limits, of mines and grazing leases. Yet, the minister can see no reason for a change now. To my mind the history of the past is the very strongest reason why we should endeavour to devise some other way whereby we could handle what belongs to the Dominion of Canada in a better way than it has been handled in the past, and to bring to the country a larger return for it.

If the regulations referred to be the regulations made under the Land Act, and if the government are exercising the power of regulating the entire question of how rights are going to be acquired under the Lands Act, by a system of regulations made by the government over a period of thirty years past, it would seem to me that the government ought to be in a position to know what are proper regulations to make, and if the government are in that position I fail to see why they do not propose to this House to enact those regulations into law. I understood from the minister that the Teason why it was considered necessary that the government should have conferred upon it power to control these matters, was that the whole thing was in embryo, quite a new thing, something which could not now be elaborated

and provided with a permanent system. I was struck with this position as going a great way to justify this departure from the sound principle that the control of the acquisition of these rights ought properly to be determined by this parliament, but if the government has been prescribing by regulations for a period of thirty years the manner of disposal and acquisition of similar rights I do not grasp how it could be said that the whole matter is in that embryonic condition in which it would be impossible to formulate and lay before the House just the regulations required for that purpose. There seems to me to be a contradiction between the two positions taken by the minister. Is it intended that existing regulations under the Lands Act shall govern the acquisition of the rights with which we are now dealing in this particular portion of the country that is to be set aside as a forest reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is intended that the regulations at present applicable to these rights in other sections of the country shall be made applicable to the same purposes within the proposed reserve, but with such changes as are considered necessary in order to carry out the special purpose of this reservation. It is the special purpose of this reservation that makes the new condition which is not thoroughly understood and which makes it impossible to apply the regulations as they are, and have been in use in the rest of the country. My hon. friend argues that we should have our regulations which apply to the country "genera ally put in statutory form, but the underlying principle of these regulations, in regard to mineral rights particularly, was reversed in 1907 and 1908 so that the present regulations have only been in force since that time. They have not been thoroughly worked out, and the fact that they were reversed in 1907 and 1908 from the regulations prevailing before is evidence of what I have already said that in the formative condition it is desirable that there should be a freer means of meeting new conditions and new situations as they arise than is provided by definite legislation.

As I understand, the regulations already made under the Lands Act must not only be submitted to parliament, but must be approved by parliament. These regulations approved by parliament have become law, and it does not seem to me desirable that what parliament has approved and made law should be susceptible to alteration not only in details, but in entire principle, as the minister says in 1907 these regulations were altered by the Governor in Council alone. I do not know how long these regulations had been in force before they were altered, but I fail to see any reason why the power should remain in the hands of the Governor in Counoil. There does not seem to me to be anything to indicate that there was such urgent need to make changes in the regulations that parliament had sanctioned that it was necessary to give that power to the Governor in Council. I have had occasion to look at some of the regulations made by order in council under the Lands Act which are before the House now.
It appears that a number of the regulations changed had been in force for a long period of years. If that is true, what is the necessity of placing the power to amend those regulations, which have become law by the action of parliament itself, in the hands of the Governor in Council? We have an annual session of parliament, and surely the few months that would elapse while the government would wait to submit to parliament any proposed alterations in those regulations, would not be a matter of vital importance. We are dealing here not with pure questions of administration. They may be questions of administration if you look at these lands as the property of the government; but you are going quite beyond that when you make a law to determine how rights in that property may be alienated and become the property of individuals; and the minister has, I think, conceded that when you are making a law for the purpose of determining how the public generally may acquire rights on certain property, the first essential is that that law should secure perfect equality of right between all citizens who arc subjected to it. Now, we- are asked, because it has been done in the past with regard to this immense tract of property, to surrender our legislative power to determine how one may acquire rights in or upon it, over to the Governor in Council; and I can see no reason for that except that between sessions of parliament there might arise a necessity for amending these laws. I have entire sympathy with the position taken by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve), that parliament ought to keep control over legislation that is to govern the transmission of this particular kind of property, just as fully as it should keep control over any other matter that is subject to its legislative competence. It seems to me that the continuance of the system under the Lands Act is difficult to justify in itself; but to so a step further, and to say that because it does exist under the Lands Act, we must continue it here, when there is no substantial reason advanced to establish the necessity of our doing so, seems to me to be very far from conclusive. In the perusal that I have had occasion to make of the regulations passed under the power conferred by the Lands Act, it has sceemed to me that many of the matters there dealt with would have been more properly dealt-

with by parliament itself; and it is a most "undesirable system to create and maintain throughout a large section of country, under which not only the executive but the legislative power is exercised by one body, that body being properly speaking the executive branch of parliament, which we are taking out of its functions and delegating to it functions which properly speaking belong to us. That seems to ine to be in principle a most undesirable state of affairs, and one which should call for some more serious reason than any that has been advanced to justify it. This is not the only instance we have had of legislation of this kind. We have had this session quite a number of Bills in which parliament has been called on to hand over its legislative powers to the executive government. All these instances, while they may be cited as precedents for our doing the same thing again, are instances of the growth of a very serious abuse. I do not profess to be familiar with the precise details of how the rights here in contemplation ought to be dealt with; but I do think that the government, which has been administering and dealing with this kind of property throughout all these territories for a long period of years, ought to be in a position to lay before us a statute that would determine how these properties ought to be disposed of. If that were done, I can realize that it might be a proper thing with regard to the details, to confide some power of making regulations to the government. Before I sit down, I would like to point out what seems to me to be a difference between these regulations and the regulations provided for in the Lands Act. While the latter regulations become law when made, they only continue in force if approved by parliament at its next session. But under section 18 of this Bill, the approval of parliament is not required. All that is required is that the regulations shall be laid before parliament at its next session. Of course, it is competent for any member to raise the question then whether these regulations should not be abrogated, but there is a substantial difference between the requirement that regulations shall be laid before parliament without parliament being required to take any action and the requirement that they must be submitted to parliament for approval. The minister has said that the position taken by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Soroule) differs materially from that taken by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve). No doubt in moving an amendment my hon. friend from North Grey is accepting the principle of the section. but he moved that amendment on the assumption that the minister had closed the door to any possible consideration of the very conclusive reasoning made by my hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) Mr. DOHERTY.
in support of the position he took, namely, that at all events before parliament should act the minister ought to submit the regulations which are to govern the disposal of these rights.

I approve this Bill so far as it means the conservation of natural resources, but it requires but little thought to understand that the legislation is of a very serious nature. Until this Act is repealed, we divest ourselves of the power of governing a kingdom-over sixteen millions of acres-not only lands, but minerals, timber, and all the wealth contained in those lands. We have to look forward perhaps, to that kingdom becoming greater in another way. Cities and towns may grow up in it. And it is all to be governed by whom? By the Governor in Council-in name; by the minister, in name: but rather by some official appointed to carry out the work in this department, such as the gentleman who rules over the timber department. This Act is to be supplemented by regulations that are to have the same power as if they were contained in the body of the Act. The Act says the regulations are to be published in the ' Canada Gazette,' and are to be submitted to parliament, There is not even an averment in the Bill that regulations will be null and void until approved by parliament-they are to be submitted, that is all. This kingdom we are giving over to an official, a hired official, perhaps a political official, who would be appointed to take charge of it. We divest ourselves not only of _ the power we have -at present for the direction and control of all its wealth, but we are giving to this official all the powers, for	all this territory	of municipalgovernments. He is to make rules and d-o everything that a municipal council could do in a very much smaller land. He is to arrange how even the fee	simple is to	be disposed
of, and the mining rights, the timber rights, the removal of stone, gravel, or sand, the pasturage of cattle, the use of hay lands and the establishment of and use of reservoirs. There may be an agricultural community there, and I suppose that even grain growing would go with the pasturage rights in the land. I think if the minister would stay his hand and afterwards come to the House with something more definite so that we might know what sort of a government the country and the people were to have, we might assist him. But I think the House would be making a mistake in passing the Bill in its present shape.

Mr, GOODEVE. I want to reiterate and make very clear my position on this matter. I would like to take up the argument of the minister when he was trying to show that a difference in principle existed between the position of the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) and my own. I think the minister did not well sustain his contention. Both the hon. member for North Grey and I contend for the one principle of absolute publicity and absolute equal rights in the disposal of these natural resources. I will take the minister's own argument. In dealing with my position, he referred to the mining law. That is the principle I have contended for. In every province of this Dominion we have statutory enactments, or mineral laws. Every prospector knows exactly the conditions under which he can stake out a mineral claim. It does not lie in the option of the minister or of the Governor in Council to say whether he shall or shall not receive that claim. The law has fixed all the conditions. That is exactly the principle I am contending for, so that when a man applies for a grazing lease he shall know the conditions under which he can obtain that lease. I think the minister scarcely realizes that he is asking in this Bill to be made a king over 25,000 square miles of territory, even a man above the king. Practically he is given power to say to one man, Go, and he goeth; and to another man, Come, and he cometh, because he will be given power to refuse that man a right or to give him a right. He will control everything except the fee simple to that land. He becomes an absolute czar of that great kingdom of 16,000,000 acres of land. I think even the Minister of the Interior should hesitate before he asks this parliament to grant him such absolute power. All I am contending for is that which has been so well advocated by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell), and the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Haggart). We want the regulations brought down in a schedule and put in this Bill. We want to know what are the conditions under which the minister proposes to dispose of these valuable assets. We are not opposing this Bill, we are supporting the minister on the principle of this Bill, but we want to make it, if possible, of [DOT]such a character that it will conserve the great natural resources of this country. I would ask the minister to allow that section to stand for further consideration, and give us some idea of the regulations he proposes to make.
Amendment (Mr. Middlebro) negatived: Yeas 17, nays 39.
On section 17: Dominion parks.

Are we to understand that the word ' reserves ' in the section Mr. HAGGART (Winnipeg).
means the reserves that are specified in the schedule as forest reserves, and are these parks to be taken exclusively out of the [DOT]forest reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I think it might possibly be made clearer because from the wording of the section it looks as if the minister were empowered to make such reserves as he liked into Dominion parks. The section says that he may ' designate ' such reserves or areas within reserves as he sees fit.' I do not insist upon it, but it seems a little ambiguous, and it might suggest that he could make any reserves he liked.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Suppose we insert the word ' forest ' before the word ' reserves '?
Yes, I think that would make it perfectly clear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I move that the word ' forest ' be inserted in the second line of section 17 between the words ' within ' and ' reserves '.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 18: regulations to be published and laid before parliament,
Is it the intention of the minister that parliament shall have any legislative authority over these regulations when they are laid before parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not the intention as [DOT]expressed in the section.
What is the use of laying them before parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For the information of parliament.
Suppose they are not satisfactory to us, what remedy have we?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will be an opportunity to express an opinion with regard to them, and I presume that if the opinion be well founded it would be for the government to try to meet the opinion so expressed and if the majority in parliament should disagree with the regulations it would be for the government to step down and out.

W'ould not the minister adopt somewhat the same principle as that which he adopted in his Indian Act the other day when he gave the judge of the Exchequer Court power to do certain things, but he must lay his report on the table of the House, and it must receive the assent of this House before it becomes operative? Would it not be fair that these regulations should not become operative until assented to by parliament. Sure-

ly, when a minister is going to make regulations under which he has power to dispose of millions and millions of dollars worth of the assets of this country, we should have some say as to the manner in which they should be disposed of. Under the sections that we have passed already he will have absolute authority, and this parliament will have nothing whatever to do with the matter of disposing of these assets. Surely the minister will not prevent parliament from having some say, from giving consent to the manner in which these assets shall be disposed of. It is merely to give the House an erroneous impression to say that these regulations shall be laid before the House, but that we shall have no legislative authority to deal with them. The whole substance of the Act is that this parliament shall have the right to say how these assets shall be disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The larger part of the regulations would be of such a character and for such a special purpose that I do not think it would be for the dignity of parliafnent to require parliament's consideration of or assent to them. If my hon. friend will read sections 16 and 17 he will see that regulations are required for a very large number of what might be considered trivial matters, and I would hardly think that it would be necessary or desirable that these matters should be subject to the approval of parliament. I do not think it would add to the dignity or prestige of parliament that it should be so. With regard to the regulations for the disposal of natural resources, these are the important ones, and I have no doubt these are the ones that my hon. friend had specially in mind. With regard to regulations such as already exist, and which are applied to Dominion lands generally undeA the control of the Dominion government, these regulations are subject to the approval of parliament, as my hon. friend desires. The application of these regulations to the forest reserve area will only mean certain restrictions or modifications so as to bring them into line with the special purpose for which the reserve is set apart. The basic principle of the alienation of the public right in these resources will already have been approved by parliament as being embodied in the original regulations which are general in their application throughout the country, and therefore it would seem to me unnecessary that the adaptation of these regulations to the park reserves should, in the same degree, be submitted to parliament.

The minister does not say that the regulations regarding the forest reserves will be the same as those provided under the Dominion Lands Act with
regard to other sections of the country. We have a Bill before the House now with regard to orders in council that have already been passed under the Dominion Lands Act. These regulations are all submitted to, and approved by parliament. The minister might put in force a certain regulation under the Dominion Lands Act which might have been approved by parliament, and then he might turn around and put in force an entirely different regulation under the Forests Reserves Act, with which he does not require to come before parliament at all. If he puts it in this Bill that these regulations are to be the same as those under the Dominion Lands Act, which are already approved by parliament, that is one thing, but to take to himself authority to make entirely different regulations without the approval of parliament is something with which we cannot agree.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It certainly is not the intention to make different regulations. I have already explained that it is the intention to adapt the regulations that are generally applicable to the special conditions which prevail in the parks and reserves. If these regulations have already been approved by parliament it does not seem to me necessary that the adaptation should also require the approval of parliament. It is true, as my hon. friend says, that the Act does not say the regulations shall be the same. The Act cannot say that the regulations shall be the same and yet may be different. I can assure the House there is no intention to exercise the power my hon, friend suggests may be exercised. Our idea is to have the regulations throughout the country, whether in or out of reserves, conform as closely as possible in their general principle, but we have to vary them, for instance, in the case of school lands, which are a trust, and in the case of park reserves.

lations shall be laid before both Houses of parliament within the first fifteen days of the session next after the date thereof, and such regulations shall remain in force until the day immediately succeeding the day of prorogation of that session of parliament, and no longer, unless during that session they are approved by resolution -of both Houses of parliament.
That is a reasonable section, and I would ask the minister what objection he could have to inserting it here?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have explained that many of the matters calling for regulations under this Act are not of sufficient importance to deserve the careful scrutiny given to a legislative enactment. The transactions covered by the Dominion Lands Act are of a much more important character than the regulation of the conduct of persons in a park for instance. While my successor might not he bound by what I say, if he should place before the House regulations in regard to parks not conforming in their basic principles to the regulations existing:, he would lay himself open to strong criticism by the House.

Is there any difference between the powers given in this Act in regard to the alienation of public property and the powers given in the Dominion Lands Act, except that under the Forest Reserves Act the fe'e of the land cannot be sold or alienated?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a stupendous difference, and is one of the great reasons why we do not need to look at one in exactly the same light as the other.
A license to cut timber or remove ore is as much an alienation as the issue of a patent. The timber is the land, so is the ore.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would not like to become involved in a dispute with my hon. friend in regard to law, but in administration under the Lands Act we do not recognize that timber is land. Where a timber license is granted we retain the right of entry on the the land for mineral or other purposes, the. licensee has only a right of access to the land for the timber, and for the beneficial use of that timber for his own purposes.

There are places where the timber is worth many times the value of the land on which it grows, and the real estate consists of the land with the timber on it. If there is $9 worth of timber for every dollar's worth of land, the minister could alienate and dispose of the $9 worth of timber under this Act without submitting it to parliament, whereas he cannot deal with a dollar's worth of the land itself. What objection can there be to his laying before parliament orders in council that may be made under the Forests Reserve Act at the same time that he brings down Mr. PERLEY.
the regulations made under the Dominion Lands Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that there is any objection to it, but I am arguing in defence of the Bill as drafted, that there is no reasonable necessity for doing so. What my hon. friend said about the alienation of the timber is not the question, the alienation of the timber does not have to be laid before parliament, it is the regulations under which that alienation takes place.

If I followed the minister rightly, none of these regulations, either in the respect in which they would be identical with the regulation^ under the Lands Act nor in the respects in which they may differ from them, would be submitted to parliament for its approval.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not as the Bill stands.
Mr. DOHERTYL As pointed out, the alienation of the right to cut timber or to extract minerals may be the alienation of a very much more valuable thing than the fee simple in the land itself, and if it was considered desirable under the Lands Act that we should make regulations to govern the alienation of land, if it was a proner thing that these regulations should only continue to have force after having had the approval of parliament, why is it not just as important to have that requirement with regard to regulations governing the alienation of rights which in a large number of cases are of much more value than the land itself? I admit that there is force in the statement that it might be beneath the dignity of parliament t0' be dealing with regulations on trivial matters; but that would not irrevent a provision being made that would require regulations made under the powers conferred by subsection (b) of section 16 to be subject to the same requirement that is made with regard to the alienation of land under the Lands Act. Apparently every regulation made under the Lands Act requires the approval of parliament. Even if the minister, by a general regulation under this Act, should make the regulations made under the Lands Act applicable, and later on should proceed to alter those regulations under the Lands Act, the alterations would have to be submitted to the approval of parliament; but that would not necessarily apply to the provisions of this new Act. So that you would have a situation in the future where the minister, if he took the regulations under the Lands Act and made them the regulations under this Act, would have to submit them to parliament for approval, whenever he allowed them as regulations' under that Act, whereas as regulations under this Act, they would not require the approval of parliament. Is there any reason for that distinction? Whereas you refuse to make a law that will last longer

than the next session of parliament of any regulation under the Lands Act, you give the minister absolute carte blanche to make regulations governing every matter coming under this Act, without coming to _ parliament at all. If parliament is going to dispossess itself of legislative power over these matters, it ought at least to do it in accordance with some consistent system, and upon some basis that will indicate that we are not doing it by pure haphazard. Apart from that mere argument of inconsistency, it does seem that the power to deal with these important rights is such a wide power that it would be only proper, if parliament should have nothing to say before the regulation is made and goes into force, it should at least be given the power to sanction or refuse sanction after it has been done, unless for some reason it is considered desirable that the government should be put in a position where in regard to these matters it shall be absolutely beyond the control of parliament, even though parliament is in session and is in a position to deal effectively with them. I would submit that it would be only a proper recognition of parliament that the regulations should at least, after they have come into force, be submitted to parliament for approval. Moreover, this would put us in the position of being consistent with previous legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no serious objection, from my point of view, to adopting the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Anne. To my mind it is not necessary either to maintain the dignity of par-lfament or to preserve the public rights in the matter; but there is no objection to it, and I would be quite willing to add to this section such a provision as my hon. friend has suggested. I still think that the Act would be just as well without that provision and the public interest just as well served, but I am quite willing to defer to my hon. friend's view.

I move in amendment:
Every regulation made by the Governor in Council in virtue of the provisions of subsection 'B/ section 16, shall have force and effect only after it has been published for four consecutive weeks in the 'Canada Gazette.'
Then add the terms of the Dominion Lands Act.

speechtext:
Perhaps it would be just as well to let this section stand, and I shall have a section drafted to' be placed before the committee later on.

I would like to draw attention to a question regarding the boundary between Southern Alberta and British Columbia. I think it is generally conceded that it i-s not laid down correctly in the maps. A person convicted within the province of Alberta might be found later to have been in the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The boundary between Alberta and British Columbia is not well defined, and in process of time we shall no doubt get a better definition. Generally speaking, however, the best guide as to what constitutes the boundary is the flow of water. The map is wrong, but on the ground the flow of water would be the best direction to ascertain whether an individual was in British Columbia or Alberta.

In the schedule there are two reserves left out, namely, the Donald forest reserve and the Lake Manitoba forest reserve. Why are these left out?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The reason why the Donald forest reserve was left out was because it has a very considerable quantity of land suitable for settlement, and the timber on it is not of much value; and instead of occupying an elevated wood area, which would be a source of water supply, the reserve is chiefly in the vallev of the Columbia river. I would therefore, move to add to the schedule the Nesbitt forest reserve.

speechtext: I understand from the premier's reading that there is not a definite statement that they will not continue, they simply ask that the arrangement be made for one year, so that if further arrangements are not made, they will be in a position to drop it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. I had an opportunity of discussing it with the Imperial authorities four years ago when I attended the conference. The present passage from Liverpool to Hong Kong in 25 days does not give a sufficiently rapid service for the requirements of the British people. I think the Peninsular and Oriental service is shorter, but our aim is to have a service via Canada in a shorter period than the Peninsular and Oriental can give us. We are not without hope that we shall be able to accomplish that, especially since we have not renewed our contract yet for the Atlantic service. 'But we have reason to believe that an offer will be made to us for a much faster service on the Atlantic than we have at the present time.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister if it is not a fact that by subsidizing these steamships they will bring eggs from China into the Canadian market to compete with our farmers, and if he thinks it is wise for us to subsidize steamships for that-purpose.
WILFRID LAURIER. I do not think that I would risk the service. I think I would risk the eggs rather. I think that I would keep the service even if we had a few more eggs for ourselves.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have at the present time a treaty with the United States for the suspension during a term of years of pelagic sealing. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) remembers that in 1894 Sir John Thompson attended a conference between Great Britain and the United _States for the regulation of pelagic sealing. The origin of this discussion was that the United States had seized certain of our vessels engaged in sealing operations in the northern sea, pretending that the northern sea was a mare clausum and that the sealers were fishing in American waters. We contested that contention and succeeded. At the same time it was represented to us that pelagic sealing was destroying seal life in this that the females were liable to be killed on their way to the rookeries and that the life of the seals was very much in danger because for every female that is killed two lives are sacrificed. Whatever may be said of this contention, which seemed to me to be founded in fact, we agreed to two things, first, that pelagic sealing, which is sealing on the high seas and which has been engaged in principally by sealers from Victoria, should be restricted to certain seasons. I think it was from February up to a certain time in June, but I forget the months. At all events, there was to be a close season during which our sealers were prohibited from sealing. They were prohibited frcm using shot guns and were compelled to use only the harpoon. Then, they did not have the right to seal up to the three mile

limit around the Pribyloff Islands but they were restricted to a zone of seventy miles from the islands. This has gone on for some years. Now, a new class of sealers has come into existence carrying the Russian and Japanese flags and these Russian and Japanese sealers can seal at all times without observing any close season, they can use all sorts of weapons and they have the whole field to themselves without any restriction.
Not restricted to any zone?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They have no zone tp observe. They have been destroying seal life and there is a possible danger of the seal disappearing as the [DOT] buffalo has disappeared. We are to have a conference which is to open on the 11th of this month at Washington between Great Britain, the United States, Russia and Japan and in the meantime we have made an arrangement with the United States by which it is provided that if the operation of killing seals on the Pribyloff Islands is carried on within fifteen years we shall have 20 per cent of the catch. If the Americans killed on their own territory 100,000 seals or 50,000 seals we would have 20 per cent of the catch and other considerations which will be found valuable but which I would not like to disclose at this moment. Mr. Bryce is to be the chief commissioner of Great Britain and we have appointed as our chief commissioner Mr. Joseph Pope who is quite familiar with the whole subject having accompanied Sir John Thompson and Sir Charles Tupper to Paris in 1894. He has already left for Washington and he has taken with him Mr. Found of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. Macoun, of the Geological Survey, who was at Paris in 1894 and who knows the subject thoroughly from the point of view of the naturalist. Capt. Byers represents the sealers of Victoria,
