I understand that members of parliament who are invited to go are merely invited (by a committee of members of parliament in England, and that they are to be entertained privately or in some semi-official way by members of the English House of Commons. Had this been brought before the House before Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
the selection of members I certainly should have opposed any limited number of men going in this way. There will be more than 18 members of the House of Commons and Senate of Canada in England, and with all due regard to the gentlemen selected-and I may say a number of the names especially, of my good friend on my left (Mr. Foster), and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart), and the gentleman who represents the west on our side are very good names and the maritime province representative-but I have no hesitation in stating that had this been understood at the time as it is now understood there would have been a different story to be told. I do not think, in the first place, that any number should have been selected, but that every man who goes over there should be on an equal footing, and if he pays his own expenses I think he should be as highly regarded in the old country as here. I am not speaking personally, I am going under other auspices, and possibly it is invidious for me to take this stand, but I am doing so on principle. I do not know what attention will be paid to these gentlemen over there. There are five members from the Conservative side and seven or eight from the government side who are to go over on this delegation. Those not on that delegation will have the privilege of paying for seats and watching the performance from a fence corner while others will be entitled to certain favours. More than that when this matter was discussed, it was distinctly understood on this side of the House that each man would go at his own cost. Now a number of gentlemen are quite, disappointed. Had this $1,000 grant been known then I am satisfied a number of gentlemen would have consented to let their names go in for selection, who did not see their way clear to pay their expenses. Were the invitation official from the imperial government to this, for these members to go I would not hesitate. I do not see why the country should pay the expenses of gentlemen who are not invited officially. I do not think the item should be asked for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As has been stated by my hon. friend the invitation that was sent to us was not official, it was simply an invitation of a committee of members of the House of Commons addressed to us. We would have preferred that they should have made their own selection and sent them their invitation, but the invitation had to come through some channel, and it came through the channel of the Canadian government. When we received the invitation we had to follow strictly the terms in which it was couched, and the request was to invite 18 members of our parliament,

Could we not have courteously told them that we respectfully regretted having to decline their invitation inasmuch as many more than 18 would be there and the government' could not take it on themselves to make any invidious distinction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think we could do that, they might have invited 18, or 20 or 45, but they invited 18 and I do not think we should have made any observations, we could not say we will not accept that unless you invite all our members. The invitation having been received and being meant to be courteous we accepted it as courteously, and we think that under all the circumstances it is better that the Canadian parliament should provide for their expenses. I do not agree with my hon. friend as I have sometimes the pleasure of agreeing with him.
At the time word was passed around it was stated there would be no cost to the country, that no members were to be paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was rumoured; certainly it was not officially stated.

I was asked if I wished to go to the old country on that occasion or not, and I was led to understand I would have to pay my own expenses. I accepted and said I would go at my own expense. ________________; [DOT]	~	*	"

I find myself in a rather awkward position about this vote, and would like to put it as right as I can. Last fall when it. was first rumoured that some of the members of parliament would be asked specially to go to the coronation it was said that some allowance would be made by this parliament towards their expenses, in the same way that Australia and New Zealand were doing. Later in the session it was stated in the corridors that this idea was given up and that no vote would be asked towards the expenses of the members of the House of Commons and the Senate, who might go to the coronation. One day the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) sent for me and said that the Prime Minister had called at his office and told him that an invitation had been received from a committee of the House of Commons in England, asking that 18 members of the Canadian parliament should be named to whom this committee in England would simply show courtesy. This was not an official committee of the English parliament, but as I understood it a certain number of the members of the House of Commons who wished to show some attention to the members of parliament from overseas, had decided to ask them in this way, and it
was proposed to give them trips into the historical portion of England, and I suppose some dinners and other entertainments. The Prime Minister then, as I understood, told the leader of the opposition that the selection of names had to be made within a day or two. The leader of the opposition asked me to try to find out what members from our side of the House intended to go to the coronation. He said there were no expenses to be paid by parliament, and no allowances to be made, and I took it that he got this understanding from the Prime Minister himself. Therefore, we went to the various members on our side of the House, and asked them if they intended to go to the coronation. I was asked by some members, as were other whips, why we were asking this question. We told them that the arrangement, as we understood it, was that no expenses were to be paid or allowances voted by this parliament, but that this private committee of the House of Commons of England were to have certain names of members given to them who would be more or less official and to whom these courtesies would be shown. After we got the names of those who on our side of the House intended to go to the coronation anyway,the leader of the opposition topk the list and chose the ones from each section who had been the longest in the House. That was the way the selection was made. A few days afterwards it was rumoured that the government intended to ask for a grant for an allowance to these gentlemen, and I might say that it placed us all in a very awkward position, because, although the names given in by the leader of the opposition are representative and satisfactory names, at the same time I happen to know of one or two of our older members who would have liked to have gone to the coronation, and might have done so if they had known that there was going to be a grant by parliament for that purpose. They did not feel able to go at their own expense entirely. While I have no desire to make any objection to this vote, I want to say to the Prime Minister that I think the way this matter has been handled has not been a fair deal at all, because if it was the intention of the Prime Minister to ask for a vote from this House for this purpose, it should have been communicated to the leader of the opposition at the time that he asked him to give the names of five members on this side of the House for that purpose. I wish simply to make this explanation in order that I may put myself right in the matter.

I differ a little from a good many who have spoken. I am pretty well satisfied with this matter. I think it is a matter that we should leave altogether to the responsibility of the government. They propose to pay what would be equivalent to the expenses of these gentlemen if

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: they are not too extravagant, and I think we can leave that to them, to do as they dike about it. I was asked if I would like [DOT]to go, and when I was asked that I took for granted that the expenses would be paid. I said no. I did not want to go; so I am not at all disappointed. I did not want to go when I thought my expenses would be paid. I would not give any different reply if I were asked now. If we were at the beginning of this affair, I am not at all sure that I would be in favour of having the expenses paid; I rather think I would not. 3 am satisfied with the gentlemen who have been selected, for a very good reason, that I do not know exactly who they are, with the exception of two or three, and I have not gone to the trouble of finding out. But in this parliament I think we could hardly go wrong in making a selection of men who would be well qualified to represent ns on this occasion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would be very sorry if my hon. friend from Argen-teuil thought that the manner in which this matter had been conducted had not been fair. Certainly nothing was more removed from my intention. I wanted to be absolutely fair to everybody. I cannot recall minutely what passed between the hon. leader of the opposition and myself. I communicated to him the parliamentary communication which had been received by us from the parliament of Great Britain. I have no recollection that at that time the matter of expenses was mentioned at all. Later on it was mentioned, and there were opinions expressed pro and con as to whether the expenses should be paid or not. There were divided opinions on both sides of the House. For my part I took the liberty of nonsuiting a few personal friends both on this side and on the other side of the House, and having got the opinions of several members on which I thought I could Tely, I submitted the matter to my colleagues, and here is the result. I think on the whole the action was well taken, and should receive the approval of everybody.

The item under consideration is not a very large item in itself. To my mind, however, it acquires an additional significance by reason of the fact that the beneficiaries are members of this House. The question before us has a double aspect: First of all, the aspect so far most commented on in the debate, namely, the manner in which the recipients of this grant were selected from among ourselves. That to my mind is not a very important feature of the case. It may be that unfairness has been the result of the method adopted. To my mind we should fight that out, if it has occurred, among ourselves, independently altogether of out relationship as members of parliament.

That is to say, it should not be a subject for discussion in the House. The feature, though, in which the country is and should be interested is this: Is it a proper principle to vote the money of the country for this purpose? That to my mind is all that is open for us to discuss here. Now, it seems that the invitation has arisen at the instance of certain citizens of the British Empire who are members of the British parliament. Those men got together, and determined that their hospitality as private individuals should be extended to certain members of the Canadian parliament. It is to be noted that they have no official position in extending that hospitality. They are merely private citizens who happen to be members of parliament. The British government does not come into the matter at all, or ask that this country be officially represented by members of this House. The Prime Minister states that although that is the case, they chose the channel of the Canadian government to carry the invitation to the members of this House, and he assumes that that puts a different aspect on the invitation, gives it a semi-official character, and justifies the government in voting the money of the people to pay the expense. I am at a loss to understand how they could have communicated the invitation in any other way. It was simply a method of communication. It did not change in any way the character of the communication. It did not lift it out of the category of a purely private extension of hospitality, and make it in any way official or semi-official.
That was the method they chose, but the invitation remained all the while just the private invitation of members of the Imperial House. That being the case, it became, to my mind, the duty of members of this House to decide whether or not they should respond, and not the duty of the government. The members of this House did respond. Surely at that point the matter should end. I do not see any justification for voting the people's money to pay the expenses in any degree whatever. It does not matter what the understanding was, the reason of the trip is of a personal and not a public character, and I do not see how this invitation differs from that which many citizens throughout Canada are accepting from their friends across the water. I cannot see the distinction. If a distinction can be pointed out, I am open to change my mind, but until it is, I must oppose the vote. It appears to me utterly indefensible. It is not pleasant to take exception to a vote of this kind. Nobody would take exception to the members who have been selected, and I hope no on.e will imagine that I had any expectation of going "myself. I could not go no matter who paid tiie expenses, and further it would not

be a great object to me in any event. T take more pleasure meeting the common people in my constituency than those by whom perhaps I would be entertained over there. But I would like any member of this House to show me what there is in this invitation, and its acceptance that will justify this vote ox place those who accept the invitation in a different position from other Canadians attending the coronation. The representatives of the government are in a different position, because they go as the official representatives of Canada, and it is only right that the Canadian people should pay their expenses, but this item is of an entirely different character, and I can see no defence whatever for the vote.

I wish to say a word with reference to this item. I think I have stood for some 25 or 30 years in this parliament as a fair defender of economy; and in this instance I have no hesitation at all in saying that under all the circumstances I should defend the vote. But I also feel it is my duty at present to move myself entirely from the category of those who will benefit by it, and I shall, therefore, tomorrow morning hand in my resignation as one of those selected by the hon. leader of the opposition. I shall support the vote. Nothing would have made me happier than to have had visited the old country under these circumstances, but I am not able to pay my own way and shall therefore forego that pleasure, and under the circumstances shall remove myself from the list of those who were deputed_to attend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I trust my hon. friend (Mr. Foster), will reconsider his decision.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: While I realize that this, like every other expenditure of public money, is a legitimate subject for public discussion, and consequently have no fault to find with the views of hon. gentlemen who oppose it, I do not believe there is a citizen of the Dominion who, on serious reflection, will object to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), receiving this small allowance. He has been in the public life of Canada a long time. He is one of the oldest members of this House, and .occupies a distinguished position in it, and I do not hesitate to say that it is right and proper he should go, and the government, as a government, are entirely prepared to assume the responsibility of this vote, to say it is a proper vote, and not hold any hon. gentleman opposite responsible for it at all. I hope, therefore, that my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), will reconsider his judgment and consent to be one of the delegates.

The great objection, to my mind, in this matter, is this:	Here
are 18 members selected from this House of Commons, and these gentlemen, when they cross the water, will be the guests of the members of the House of Commons and the House of Lords in England. The invitation is a private one. I do not know what favours will be shown them, but I do protest, and shall continue to protest, against any member from this House or another citizen from this Dominion who crosses over the water, not having the favours shown him that these gentlemen will have. Here is my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Smyth) going across and paying his own expenses. He will stand among the crowd, and he is equally a representative of the people, and what I object to is that any member who goes across and pays his own expenses should not have the same recognition as any other member whose expenses are paid. That is the ground I take. I am not begrudging the money, I have never been a cheese parer, but i do not see why any member of parliament should be entitled to any special favour over there because he happened to be chosen as a delegate on the invitation of a number of gentlemen on the other side, and be given prominence over his brother members here who also attend the coronation and pay their own expenses. I am surprised that such a proposition should be made, knowing it would certainly bring hard feelings into the hearts of men who pay their own expenses and have to take pot luck, while these hon. gentlemen are given the favours. If the right hon. the Prime Minister will see that any favours that may be conferred on these 18 gentlemen will be extended to the others who pay their own expenses and are not costing the country a dollar, I shall make no opposition. With me it is a question of principle, a question of giving fair play to all, and that is the reason why I am opposing, not the vote, but the principle on which it is based.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend is altogether under a misapprehension. The matter which he discusses has nothing to do with the payment or non-payment of the members chosen to represent parliament. Whether they be paid or not, they have been selected by the two sides as those who should accept the invitation from the committee of the Houses of Commons and Lords. With that I have nothing at all to do. I shall be in England as the official representative of the Canadian people, if I may say so, and every member of parliament, invited or not, is the same to me. Anything that I can do to have the favour shown to him to which he is entitled I shall be most happy to do, and I shall not make any distinction between those members, and the other 18. It will be my pleasure to see that all are treated alike and on the same footing. But as to these 18 members, that is a

different matter. These 18 members were chosen, but they will not be there officially any more than the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Smyth), who says he will go and pay his own expenses. These 18 members will be the guests, not of the whole parliament of Britain, but of a committee of members of the House of Commons. That is altogether a private affair. With regard to the other question, I hope that my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) will follow the advice given by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding), and that he will consider himself invited. I think it would be a pity if my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) was not there. Some time ago, speaking publicly, I expressed regret that Mr. Deakin, who was Prime Minister of Australia at the time of the last conference, had not been selected as one of the members to represent Australia. I hope he will be there, as I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Foster will be there.
At his own expense, while the others are paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The eighteen members from Australia have their expenses paid by the Australian government, as the expenses of the eighteen members from Canada are to be paid by the Canadian government. I hope that my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) will be there to represent that portion of the Canadian people whom he represents so ably.

I desire, in the first place, to join most earnestly in the. observation of the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) and the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) so far as they urge upon the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) the desirability of reconsidering the decision he has made. I am sure there was no intention on the part of any hon. gentleman who spoke, whatever opinion he may have expressed, to convey any impression oi objection, or that there could be objection, to the hon. member for North Toronto, as one of those who accepted this invitation.
I did not even know who composed the delegation.

Nor do I] and I trust that the hon. member for North Toronto will accept the suggestion already made to him by more authoritative voices than my own, and that he will see fit to withdraw the statement he has made with regard to his intention of not accepting the invitation. I have no desire whatever to make any objection to this vote. I would like, however, to offer a suggestion in regard to the terms in which it is set forth. I make the suggestion, in view of the statement of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) with regard to the misunderstand-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
ing that seems to have occurred concerning the nature of this invitation, and which misunderstanding may possibly have had something to do with the method of determining who should be the gentlemen to accept the invitation of the committee of members of parliament on the other side. I notice that the vote is provided for the expenses of the ' parliamentary delegation.' I think, under the circumstances, that it is not absolutely correct to speak of these gentlemen as a ' parliamentary delegation.' I understood the First Minister to say a moment ago that these gentlemen will not be there in any more official capacity than any other member of the House who might be in England, and desire to attend the coronation. They are going, as I understand it, .as accepting an invitation from certain members of parliament on the other side, not, properly speaking, as an official delegation from this parliament, I do not understand that this parliament, as a parliament, took any official step to delegate them. I would suggest that there might be found a modification of the wording of the vote which would make it clear that there is not sought to make any official distinction between gentlemen who may go, other than that these gentlemen who accept the invitation given. I am not prepared, perhaps to express it exactly as it ought to be expressed, but my idea would be met if, instead of saying we were voting money to pay the expenses of a parliamentary delegation, we should say that we were voting money to pay the expenses of members of the Senate and House of Commons attending the coronation, and accepting the invitation of the committee of members of parliament on the other side. I suggest that simply to make it quite clear what I think everybody understands, that there is no intention to make these gentlemen any more official representatives than any other member of parliament who may attend. I think that is no offence to the gentlemen-if I thought it was, I would not make the suggestion. I suggest this as putting on record exactly the facts and leaving no room for misunderstanding as to the relative positions of the members who have been fixed upon to accept this official invitation, and other hon. members who mav attend the coronation.

I have the honour to be one of those nominated on this side of the House on this delegation, and, in case there should be any misapprehension about the matter, I wish to state that, so far as I know there was no information given to the delegates on our side of the House which was not given to the delegates on the other side. I did not know anything about whether there would be money provided to pay expenses or not, and the
MAY 9, 19il
first news I had of it was when I saw it in print in the estimates brought down yesterday. No pressure came from the delegation on this side, so far as I know, to have the vote put in the estimates. If I understand my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) the objection seems to be that it was not known on the other side that provision would he made to pay the expenses and that if it had been known they would have made a different selection from that which they did make.
May I correct the hon. member?
That is what it appeared-

Might I offer a remark? The statement was made to the members when the question was brought up, and each member was told: You will have to pay your own expenses. I think it went further than not being brought up, and that it was brought up in the way I state.

There seems to have been no authority on the part of anybody to make that statement. If there was any misunderstanding it must have grown up among hon. gentlemen opposite themselves. It should not be too late to rectify it. They ought to be able to agree on five gentlemen on that side to attend this delegation, and if there is any difficulty of that kind, I do not see why it could not be rectified yet, or why they could not make some selection that would suit them all. It is unfortunate if any hard feelings with regard to the selection on that side should exist. There are no such feelings on this side. I believe everybody is quite cordial, and I am glad to say that I was congratulated by nearly every friend around me when my name was given as one of those to go. I will vote against the motion when the vote is put.-I presume my hon. friends on the other side are not talking for the sake of talking, and that they intend to do something more than merely object. In that case, I will join my hon. friends and vote against it. I feel delicate about making any motion, for I do not know how it will affect the gentlemen who have accepted this invitation. I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes). If I understand this matter, the invitation comes from members of the imperial parliament, it is not a general invitation from the House of Commons of England, but from individual members, of whom Lord Rosebery is chairman. It would be natural to suppose that everybody who goes from Canada would receive attention. I suppose there will be thousands of people' from Canada in London, and it would be impossible that these can all obtain
seats in Westminster Abbey to witness the coronation. It would be impossible to grant the same privilege to everybody going from Canada. For my part, I would be inclined to move that the item be struck out.

The hon. member has spoken about hard feeling among the members; I do not think there is any hard feeling upon the part of any one member against any other member on either side of the House. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has spoken his mind as he had a right to do, honestly and frankly. But I do not think there are many members in this House, or many people in the country, who will agree with him. I do not think that the manner of the invitation from certain members of the House of Commons in England to the members here, and the fact that the representatives from Canada will be entertained by members in England, is a matter that is of any concern to us at all, or that we have a right to discuss. A11 we have a right to discuss is whether this parliament shall or shall not pay the expenses of eighteen members of this parliament to go to England. 1 think that had there been no invitation at all from the old country, it would have been proper for parliament to pay the expenses of a limited number of members of the House of Commons to go with the members of the cabinet who represent Canada in England. I do not think that all the ability that is in this House of Commons is contained in the cabinet. It would have been impossible for all the members of this House to go and for their expenses to be paid by the public; no one would have expected it. As a matter of course it did place those who had to make the choice in a delicate position. No doubt many members of the House who were not selected would have filled the positions equally well. But all could not go. The member for Algoma (Mr. Smyth'e) is one of the newer members of the House, and he and others will perhaps have an opportunity to attend a similar, occasion at a later date. One of the reasons why I justify this vote is that some of the older members of the House of Commons are going. I quite agree with all those who have spoken, that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) are certainly two men who ought to be included in any list of those who go; I think we all agree in that. I do not think there will be any bad feeling either in the House or in the country, but that there will be good feeling all round. I think the people generally will be satisfied to see this vote carried.

I do not wish it to be understood that I object to this vote, I

think it is a right and proper vote, but I do not think it has been managed in the right and proper way. I should feel badly if the hon. member for North Toronto, on account of the discussion this evening, did not take his share of this vote.
I do not think it possible to do so after the statement that the chief whip has made in the House to-night.
All I can say is that if the hon. gentleman feels hurt at any words I have uttered, it is because I have not the same power of expression that he has.
I think the hon. member knew what he was saying.

I certainly had no intention of hurting the feelings of anybody in this House. I simply wanted to put myself right in regard to this matter. I have no objection whatever to this vote, I think it is right and proper. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) said that we had no reason to think there would not be a vote. For myself I think that when the Prime Minister asked for the names of five members, and did not say anything about a vote, anybody would take it for granted that there would be no vote. That is why I felt justified in saying to the members by whom I was asked that the selection was to be made from those members who intended to go to the coronation any way. I simply rose to put myself right, and to say that a mistake was made by the Prime Minister weeks ago, or months ago, when he failed to say that he intended to bring in a vote for this purpose.

I wish to say that in my opinion the attitude taken by the member for Portage la Prairie is a perfectly correct one, and I entirely agree with what he has said. I think that the official representatives of Canada in this parliament are the members of the government who are going to the conference and the coronation.

I was pleased a week ago last Friday when I heard the Prime Minister say that he had changed his mind, and that he was going to the coronation. I believe that the Dominion of Canada has a perfect right to pay his expenses. But it was distinctly understood, at least I so understood, that any other member who went would have to pay his own expenses. I think that any member of parliament who goes to England and has his expenses paid by the people of Canada, is not doing the right thing. If the government offered to pay the expenses of all the members of this House, I think they would all volunteer to go. I did not know who were the members, with the exception of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster)
who were selected to go until he stood up here and said that he was one of them. I was not aware who they were. I do not think this government has any right to pay the expenses of these men.

I regret very much that this discussion has taken a personal turn. Members on this side of the House hold George E. Foster, of North Toronto, in the highest personal regard. There is certainly no one that we would rather see go there to represent the Conservative party and the parliament of Canada than the hon. member for North Toronto. It is not in my mind a question of the personality of the members of parliament who will go. That is not the matter under discussion. It was somewhat unfairly stated by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) a few minutes ago, that the discussion arose from any dissension with regard to the selection of the individuals. I hope he will reconsider those words, because, speaking for myself, I did not know who were chosen on either side. I want to emphasize what the right hon. Prime Minister said that these hon. gentlemen are going entirely in their private capacity, and they are accepting a private invitation. They are not representing Canada in any way, they are simply going to the old country to take part in the coronation, accepting for a certain time an invitation tendered them by gentlemen who have been members of parliament. They are not representing Canada; then, why ask the people of Canada to pay their expenses? It is the principle to which I object most strongly, and if I have an opportunity I will vote against the proposal. If it carries I sincerely hope that my hon. friend from North Toronto will reconsider his determination.

I do not know that 1 can agree in every particular with my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Campbell), who has just taken his seat. Inasmuch as. members have been selected from the respective parties and the Senate to go as the representatives of these two Houses to the old country, I cannot agree altogether with the view that they in no sense will represent Canada. As I understand an invitation has come to this country from the members, of the parliament of Great Britain.
No, from private members.

I am stating it as I understand it, and if I am wrong, somebody can correct me when I get through. As 1 understand it an invitation has been sent here from the members of the British House of Commons to a number of men to go from these two Houses and be their guests while in the old country. If that is correct, then they would to a certain extent be the repre-

sentatives of Canada. But whether that is true or not, I do not agree with the principle of making this grant, I have not one word to say against the personnel of the gentlemen selected from the two parties, because I doubt if you could get a better representation of the House of Commons and the Senate, but I do not think that' the principle is a right one, and I wish simply to put on record my protest against the vote.

As I understand the situation, an invitation having come from the Imperial parliament to send 18 representatives from the parliament of Canada, a selection was made in the best judgment of the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition. They go to represent Canada whether they were invited to go or not, which is neither here nor there. They are directed by this parliament to go there for that purpose, they go with the permission of this parliament to represent this country, and if that is so why should their expenses not be borne by this country.
How does this parliament direct them?

They are directed by this parliament when we pass this estimate. We directed them when the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition agreed upon the matter, and this being the case I cannot understand why hon. members in this House will permit votes to go through for such matters as the Newmarket canal, and then rise and protest against an expenditure of $18,000 to send a delegation from this parliament to appear at the coronation of our gracious Lord, the King. To say that this is a private invitation is not meeting the situation fairly. His Majesty is not issuing invitations personally. The authority is vested in certain members of the Imperial parliament. It may be as informal as you wish, but when that invitation arrives here, and when our representatives are selected with the best judgment of the leader of the opposition and the leader of the government, I cannot understand why the country should not assume the obligation of paying their expenses just as they pay the expenses of hon. members for serving here throughout the session. No one on this side of the House deplores more than I do the discussion that has taken place here to-night. In my judgment it would have been perhaps a proper subject for a caucus to have discussed, and I am quite certain that hon. members upon reflection will realize that this is not a matter to be dealt with in the manner in which it has been handled to-night. Some of us might like to have gone ourselves. There is nothing to debar any of us from going. The hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Smyth)
deplores that he will be obliged to pay his own expenses.
I did not deplore that, because I had agreed to do it.
Then he deplores that he will have to stand behind the line and look through.
I deplore that I am not put on the same standing as some of my fellow members. I represent Canada just the same as they do.

Another hon. member wonders, if an invitation were offered, and if $1,000 were contributed to pay their expenses, how many of them would go? The same could be said of members of the bar on the opposite side of the House. If the question were put, how many of them would take a seat on the Supreme Court bench at a salary of $7,000 a year, I do not think there would be one member of the bar sitting on the other side of the House who would not hold up his hand for it. 1 think that if the House were asked how many members would go if the country offered them $1,000 to pay their expenses, probably every member who could afford the time would go. But that is not the course that has been pursued. When the leaders of both parties have exercised their best judgment in the selection of representatives of this parliament I think it is only fitting that the country should bear their expenses.

^Seeing that hon. members on both sides are taking a fling at myself, I think it due that I should say a word with regard to the matter. When I was approached and asked whether I would go to England it was emphasized very strongly that I would have to pay my own expenses. I said: Yes, I will go and when I was asked: Are you sure to go?-I said: Yes, I will go. I was under no misapprehension at all, I knew that I would have to pay my own expenses, and I was willing to pay my own expenses. I do not see why any one else should have his expenses paid when I was ready and willing to pay my own.
Salaries and expenses of the Paris agency- Further amount required, $5,500.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have appointed a new agent at Paris. My hon. friend knows that Mr. Fabre, the late agent, was paid by this parliament $6,500 and $2,000 additional which was contributed by the Quebec government. We have not thought it advisable to accept any contribution from the Quebec government, and we have made the salary of Mr. Roy, the new agent, $8,000. Mr. Fabre received no allowance whatever for contingencies; every-

thing came from the sum of $6,500. It is now proposed to provide $5,000 for office rent, and such contingencies as are necessary to carry on the work.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, House adjourned at 12.41 a.m. Wednesday.

Wednesday, May 10, 1911.
